Aphid Lion to Lacewing

Chrysoperla rufilabris is a green lacewing found in North America. Its larva has large curved mouthparts, impales aphids and sucks out their body contents. It later spins a cocoon and emerges as a pale green, winged adult.

The larva and its prey

The larvae of Chrysoperla rufilabris are predators. They pass through three instars, and they have legs and large, curved, paired mouthparts. They impale aphids and suck out the body contents.

Sources: [1] [2]

From stalked egg to winged adult

Eggs are laid singly on silken stalks on foliage. A mature larva spins a round silken cocoon, and the pupa develops before the adult emerges.

Adults are pale green, with golden eyes, long antennae and transparent wings. Adult size is roughly 12 to 20 mm. While the larvae are predators, Chrysoperla adults feed on nectar, pollen and honeydew.

Sources: [1] [2]

Where it is found

Chrysoperla rufilabris is a green lacewing found in North America. The humid habitats where it is found include irrigated crops and greenhouses.

Sources: [1]

The generalized internal view

The internal anatomy in the infographic is a generalized insect body plan, not one specific to this lacewing. Spiracles admit air into branching tracheae, the alimentary canal carries food, and the ventral nerve cord runs along the body.

Milky Seas — The Ocean’s Steady Living Glow

Milky seas are rare expanses of ocean that give off a steady whitish glow at night. Luminous bacteria are implicated, but the conditions that produce the glow remain uncertain.

At a glance

What it is
Steady whitish marine bioluminescence, visible at night
How common
Rare
Implicated source
Luminous bacteria
Duration
May persist for days to weeks
Seen from orbit
By the VIIRS day-night band, under favorable conditions

A steady glow, not a flash

Milky seas are rare expanses of steady, whitish marine bioluminescence that are visible at night. The glow may persist for days to weeks and drift with surface currents. Its steadiness sets it apart from the bioluminescence of dinoflagellates, which is mechanically stimulated and typically flashes briefly.

Sources: [1] [2]

The bacterial explanation

Luminous bacteria are implicated in milky seas. A milky sea sampled in 1985 contained luminous bacteria associated with microalgae. At high bacterial population density, chemical quorum sensing can trigger bacterial luminescence. The precise ecological relationships of the bacteria, and the conditions that produce milky seas, remain uncertain.

Sources: [1] [2]

Detecting the glow from orbit

The VIIRS day-night band can detect the faint glow from orbit under favorable conditions. Moonlight and clouds can complicate detection.

Sources: [1] [2]

The Deep Ocean Carbon Pump

Sinking particles carry organic carbon from the sunlit surface of the ocean toward the deep. The carbon starts with phytoplankton, the particles feed deep-sea life, and some carbon reaches deep waters and sediments.

At a glance

Starts with
Sunlit phytoplankton converting carbon dioxide into organic carbon
Sinking particles

Direction
From surface waters toward the deep ocean
Food for
Deep-sea animals and seafloor organisms
Storage

Carbon captured at the surface

In sunlit water, phytoplankton use photosynthesis to convert carbon dioxide into organic carbon. Phytoplankton can aggregate into sinking particles known as marine snow. Zooplankton eat phytoplankton and produce fecal pellets that contain carbon, and these pellets also sink.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the sinking particles deliver

Sinking particles transport organic carbon from surface waters toward the deep ocean. Marine snow provides food to deep-sea animals and to organisms on the seafloor.

Some of the carbon reaches deep waters and sediments, where it can remain stored for long periods. The infographic follows phytoplankton, marine snow and zooplankton pellets as they move organic carbon into the deep ocean.

Sources: [1] [2]

The Eastern Dobsonfly’s Hellgrammite

The eastern dobsonfly is an insect of eastern North America whose adults can exceed 3.5 inches in length. Its aquatic larva, the hellgrammite, is a flattened predator with sharp mandibles and gill tufts along its abdomen.

At a glance

The hellgrammite

The eastern dobsonfly, Corydalus cornutus, is a megalopteran in the family Corydalidae, found in eastern North America. Its aquatic larva is called a hellgrammite. The larva is flattened, dark and segmented, with three pairs of legs on the thorax and sharp mandibles. It is approximately 2 to 3 inches long.

Aquatic larvae live beneath rocks or logs in streams and prey on aquatic animals. Hooked appendages at the end of the abdomen help the hellgrammite resist the stream current.

Sources: [1] [2]

Gills along the abdomen

The larval abdomen has eight pairs of filaments along its sides, with cottony gill tufts at their bases. In insects, gills allow dissolved oxygen to diffuse into the body, and they are usually outgrowths of the tracheal system. The internal breathing diagram in the infographic is generalized.

Sources: [1] [3]

From stream to land to air

Development is by complete metamorphosis. It proceeds from egg to aquatic larva, then to a pupa on land, then to a winged adult. Larval development takes several years.

Sources: [2]

The winged adult

Adults have long antennae, three pairs of legs and two pairs of prominently veined wings, which are held over the body at rest. They can exceed 3.5 inches in length. The mandibles of males are long and sickle-shaped. Those of females are much shorter.

Sources: [1] [2]

The Scorpionfly’s Nuptial Gift

Panorpa communis is a scorpionfly of woodland edges and hedgerows in the UK. During courtship the male presents a collected insect to a female as a gift. The curved tip of his abdomen is used in mating and is not a sting.

A gift during courtship

During courtship, the male Panorpa communis presents a collected insect to a female as a nuptial gift. Scorpionflies may also offer secreted saliva.

Sources: [1] [2]

A tail that is not a sting

The curved, bulbous tip of the male's abdomen is his genitalia, used in mating. It is not a sting. The female's abdomen tapers. Panorpa scorpionflies have four patterned wings, a yellowish-brown body and a long beak that bears chewing mouthparts.

Scorpionflies are small insects. The body length of 3/8 inch applies to Panorpa generally and is not a precise measurement for this species.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

A scavenger of woodland edges

Panorpa communis is a scorpionfly in the order Mecoptera. In the UK it is found at woodland edges and in hedgerows, on nettles and brambles. Adults scavenge dead invertebrates and may take insects from spider webs.

As described for Panorpa, the eggs are laid in a moist environment. The larvae scavenge, and they pupate in soil.

Sources: [1] [2]

The generalized internal view

The internal view in the infographic is a generalized insect schematic. A digestive tract processes food and absorbs nutrients. Spiracles connect to branching tracheae that carry air. A ventral nerve cord connects the ganglia.

Health conditions · November 5, 2026

Achilles Tendinopathy — The Calf-to-Heel Connection

Achilles tendinopathy is a load-related problem of the tendon that connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. It causes pain, stiffness and swelling, and it is not the same as a complete rupture.

At a glance

Tendon
Achilles tendon, connecting the calf muscles to the heel bone (calcaneus)
Forms
Noninsertional (middle of the tendon) and insertional (heel attachment)
Contributing factors
Repetitive stress, a sudden increase in exercise, tight calf muscles
Symptoms
Morning stiffness, pain worsened by activity, swelling
Recovery
Can take months

The tendon and where it is affected

The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone, the calcaneus. It is used during walking, running, jumping and standing on tiptoes. Repetitive stress, a sudden increase in exercise and tight calf muscles can contribute to Achilles tendon problems.

Noninsertional disease affects the middle of the tendon. Insertional disease affects its attachment at the heel. Affected tendon fibers can develop tiny tears, degeneration, swelling and thickening. This is not the same as a complete rupture.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and assessment

Symptoms include morning stiffness, pain along the tendon or heel that is worsened by activity, and swelling. Assessment starts with history and examination. Imaging may be selected, and MRI is not always needed for diagnosis.

Sources: [1]

Management and recovery

Acute Pancreatitis — An Inflamed Pancreas

Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas, in which digestive enzymes can damage pancreatic tissue. It causes sudden, severe abdominal pain that needs urgent medical evaluation, and it is treated in the hospital.

At a glance

What it is
Sudden inflammation of the pancreas
Where the pancreas lies
Behind the stomach, near the duodenum
Common causes

Main symptom
Sudden, persistent, severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back
Hospital treatment

Outlook
Most people recover; severe illness can be life-threatening

The pancreas and its enzymes

The pancreas lies behind the stomach, near the duodenum. It makes insulin, and it makes digestive enzymes that normally help digest food in the intestine. Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas. In it, digestive enzymes can damage pancreatic tissue.

Sources: [1]

What causes it

Gallstones and heavy alcohol use are common causes. Gallstones can block the opening of the pancreas. Some medicines and other conditions can also cause acute pancreatitis.

Sources: [2]

Symptoms and urgent warning signs

Symptoms include sudden, persistent, severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back, along with nausea, vomiting and fever. Sudden severe persistent abdominal pain needs urgent medical evaluation. Severe pain spreading to the back, a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing warrants emergency care.

Sources: [2]

Evaluation and hospital treatment

Evaluation uses history, examination, blood tests and sometimes imaging such as CT. Hospital treatment includes monitoring, IV fluids and pain relief. Treating the cause may include gallstone surgery or support to stop drinking alcohol. Antibiotics are for infection, not a routine cure.

Most people recover, but severe illness may cause tissue death or infection and can be life-threatening. Reducing or avoiding alcohol, stopping smoking and following a clinician's dietary advice may help prevent recurrence.

Sources: [2]

Multiple Sclerosis — Myelin and Signal Disruption

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated disorder of the brain and spinal cord. Immune attacks damage the myelin coating around nerve fibers, and may damage the fibers themselves, which disrupts communication.

At a glance

Part affected
Central nervous system: brain and spinal cord
What is damaged
Myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibers
Lesions
Can occur in the brain and spinal cord and can be seen with MRI
Course
Relapses and remissions for some people; progressive worsening for others
Cause
Exact cause unclear
Cure
None currently

Myelin and nerve signals

Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disorder affecting the central nervous system, which is the brain and spinal cord. Myelin is the protective coating around nerve fibers. In MS, immune attacks damage the myelin around axons and may damage the axons themselves, disrupting communication. Demyelinated lesions can occur in the brain and spinal cord and can be seen with MRI.

The exact cause is unclear. Genetic susceptibility and environmental factors contribute. Smoking and prior Epstein-Barr virus infection are associated with increased risk, not with certainty of disease.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and course

Symptoms vary by person and by where the lesions are. Fatigue, visual problems, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or stiffness, and balance problems can occur.

Some people have relapses and remissions. Others experience progressive worsening. The course varies and cannot be predicted from a single illustration.

Sources: [1] [2]

Diagnosis and treatment

No single test diagnoses MS. A neurologist combines history and examination with MRI, and sometimes spinal fluid or other tests, while excluding other causes.

There is no current cure. Disease-modifying therapies can reduce relapses and slow progression for appropriate patients, and treatment depends on the type of disease and individual needs. Corticosteroids may speed recovery from a relapse but do not change the long-term course. Physiotherapy, tailored exercise, fatigue management and medicines for symptoms can help.

Sources: [1] [2]

Sudden symptoms and stroke

Sudden arm weakness or numbness, sudden vision loss or sudden balance problems can signal a stroke and require emergency medical help. They are not to be assumed to be MS. MS-like symptoms can have other causes and need to be checked by a clinician. General education is not diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Urinary Tract Infection — Bladder and Ascending Infection

In a urinary tract infection, bacteria, usually from the bowel, can enter through the urethra and multiply in the bladder. An untreated bladder infection can develop into a kidney infection.

At a glance

Urinary tract
Two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder and a urethra
Usual source
Bacteria, usually from the bowel
Entry route
Through the urethra to the bladder
Possible spread
An untreated bladder infection can develop into a kidney infection
Common treatment

The urinary tract and how infection starts

The urinary tract includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder and a urethra. The kidneys produce urine. The ureters carry it to the bladder, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it outside the body.

Bacteria, usually from the bowel, can enter through the urethra and multiply in the bladder. An untreated bladder infection can develop into a kidney infection. Catheters, impaired bladder emptying, pregnancy and menopause can increase the risk.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Symptoms and assessment

Symptoms are burning urination, urgency, frequency, lower abdominal discomfort and sometimes blood in the urine. Smell or dark urine alone does not establish a urinary tract infection. Clinical assessment uses symptoms and history and may include urine testing. Urine testing is not always needed.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment and urinary health

Antibiotics are often used for a bacterial bladder infection, and the guidance is to take prescribed treatment as directed. Rest and appropriate fluids may help symptoms. Cranberry products do not treat an established infection.

Not holding urine, taking time to empty the bladder and drinking appropriate fluids may help urinary health. Where a clinician has set fluid limits, those limits apply.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Signs that need urgent help

Fever or chills, back pain below the ribs, blood in the urine, pregnancy or rapid worsening warrant urgent medical advice. New confusion, marked drowsiness or difficulty speaking warrant emergency help.

Sources: [2]

Vitiligo — Loss of Pigment-Producing Cells

Vitiligo is a chronic condition in which skin loses pigment because working melanocytes, the cells that make melanin, are lost. It is not an infection and is not contagious.

At a glance

Cells involved

Common type

Loss of pigment cells

Vitiligo is a chronic condition. Pigment is lost because working melanocytes, the cells that make melanin, are lost. In the common form, non-segmental vitiligo, the immune system attacks melanocytes.

Vitiligo is not an infection and is not contagious. A family history and other autoimmune conditions can be associated with it.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it appears

In non-segmental vitiligo, white patches often appear on both sides, including the hands and face. Hair in affected areas can turn white. The extent of vitiligo and how it progresses vary.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it is diagnosed

Diagnosis uses an examination of the skin. A Wood lamp can help distinguish pigment loss, and selected patients may need thyroid testing. New pale patches call for assessment, not self-diagnosis.

Sources: [2]

Sun protection and treatment

Affected skin is vulnerable to sunburn, so high-SPF sunscreen and sun protection are important. Treatment can include topical medicines supervised by a clinician. Camouflage is optional. Response varies, and no cure is guaranteed. Support for the emotional impact can help.

Sources: [1] [2]

Acetaminophen Is Not Cat Medicine

Acetaminophen (Tylenol) must never be given to cats. A cat's liver is deficient at breaking the drug down, which makes it potentially fatal.

Why it is dangerous to cats

Acetaminophen, sold as Tylenol, must never be given to cats. A cat's liver is deficient at breaking the drug down, and that makes it potentially fatal.

Acetaminophen can damage red blood cells and reduce their ability to carry oxygen. It can also damage the liver.

Sources: [1] [2]

Signs that can appear

The American College of Veterinary Pharmacists lists signs that can include weakness, rapid or difficult breathing, blue-purple mucous membranes, vomiting, and swelling of the face or paws.

Sources: [2]

Where it turns up, and what happens next

Acetaminophen may be present in multi-symptom cold and allergy products. The same source says to keep medicines out of the reach of animals.

Suspected ingestion requires immediate contact with a veterinarian or with animal poison control, and accidental ingestion is to be reported immediately. The ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center hotline is (888) 426-4435.

Sources: [2]

Flehmen — The Cat’s Chemical-Sampling Pause

Flehmen is a pause that follows a cat's investigation of scent material. It helps chemical cues carried in fluid reach the vomeronasal organ, a paired sense organ near the roof of the mouth.

At a glance

Behavior
Flehmen, which follows investigation of scent material
Organ involved
The paired vomeronasal organ, near the roof of the mouth

What flehmen does

Flehmen follows a cat's investigation of scent material. It aids the access of fluid-borne chemical cues to the vomeronasal organ.

The vomeronasal organ is paired and lies near the roof of the mouth. Nasopalatine canals connect it with both the oral cavity and the nasal cavity.

Sources: [2]

Inside the organ

In its middle portion, the vomeronasal duct has sensory receptor epithelium on its medial side and respiratory epithelium on its lateral side. Glands, vessels, nerves and supporting cartilage surround the duct.

Sources: [1]

Main and accessory systems

Sensory neurons of the vomeronasal organ send their axons to the accessory olfactory bulb. The main olfactory epithelium detects volatile chemicals that are inhaled. The accessory system is associated with fluid-borne chemical cues. The functions of the two are not completely exclusive.

Sources: [2]

What is and is not known

Chemical communication takes part in social recognition and reproduction. How the cat's central nervous system processes these cues in detail remains incompletely understood.

Sources: [2]

Reading the Cat Food Adequacy Statement

The nutritional adequacy statement on a cat food label says whether the food is complete and balanced and which life stage it is intended for. It is a different thing from the ingredient list.

What the statement says

The nutritional adequacy statement identifies whether a food is complete and balanced, and the life stage it is intended for. A complete and balanced food is intended as a sole diet. Treats, snacks and supplements typically are not.

Sources: [1] [2]

How a food qualifies

A complete and balanced claim has to be backed in one of two ways. The food must meet an AAFCO nutrient profile, or it must pass a feeding trial that uses AAFCO procedures.

Sources: [2]

Not the ingredient list

The ingredient list is a separate part of the label. Its ingredients are ordered by decreasing weight, and it is not the nutritional adequacy statement.

Sources: [1]

What cats need from food

Cats need protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, fatty acids and amino acids. More supplementation is not automatically better. The Cornell guidance is to choose a food that is appropriate to the cat, with veterinary guidance. The infographic is general education, not a diet plan for an individual cat.

The Defensive Crouch in Context

A defensive cat may crouch low with its head tucked and its tail curved around or tucked under its body. The crouch is one of a cluster of signals, and a pose alone does not establish its cause.

What the posture looks like

A defensive cat may crouch low with its head tucked and its tail curved around or tucked under its body. Ears flattened sideways or backward, and wide eyes with dilated pupils, can accompany defensive postures.

Hissing and raised fur may accompany fear-related defensive behavior. Not every sign must be present in a cat that is behaving defensively.

Sources: [1] [2]

Reading the signs together

The guidance is to read the body posture, face, ears and tail together, and to consider the events that came before. A pose alone does not establish its cause.

Sources: [1] [2]

Space, and when a veterinarian is involved

Fear-related aggression can escalate if a cat cannot escape. The ASPCA guidance is not to touch, restrain or punish a cat that is displaying defensive aggression, and to give it space until it is calm.

Pain or medical problems may contribute to aggression. According to the sources, new or persistent changes warrant veterinary assessment.

The Feline Shoulder — Muscle Layers Around the Scapula

The muscles around a cat's shoulder blade, the scapula, lie in layers. The rhomboideus sits beneath the trapezius, the serratus ventralis is a deep fan-shaped muscle on the side of the trunk, and the latissimus dorsi covers part of the chest wall.

At a glance

Animal
Domestic cat

Trapezius and rhomboideus

The trapezius extends from the midline of the back to the spine of the scapula, the shoulder blade. The rhomboideus lies deep to the trapezius, that is, beneath it. It attaches to the dorsal border of the scapula.

Sources: [1] [2]

Serratus ventralis and latissimus dorsi

The serratus ventralis is a deep, fan-shaped muscle on the side of the trunk. It has a neck part and a thoracic part. The latissimus dorsi covers part of the chest wall. It lies superficial to deeper shoulder structures, which means nearer the surface.

Sources: [1] [2]

Chest muscles and a small clavicle

The pectoral muscles occupy the underside of the chest. Both superficial and deep layers are present. The cat also has a small clavicle, or collarbone, which lies in the brachiocephalicus at the shoulder.

Sources: [1] [2]

Cat Atlas / Coats and genetics · November 6, 2026

White Spotting — Unpigmented Patches

White spotting in domestic cats leaves patches of coat without pigment, from tiny marks to extensive white areas. It is associated with an insertion in the KIT gene and is distinct from Dominant White.

At a glance

Trait
White spotting in the domestic cat, Felis catus
Extent
Tiny white patches to extensive white areas
Why patches are white
The skin there lacks melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells
Associated with
A feline endogenous retrovirus insertion in KIT intron 1
Not the same as
Dominant White

How much white

White spotting ranges from tiny white patches to extensive white areas. The cats on the infographic are examples of that range. They are illustrations, not a scale of genotypes.

Sources: [1]

Why the patches have no color

The white areas lack skin melanocytes, the cells that produce pigment. This is different from a failure to make pigment. In white spotting, the pigment-producing cells are missing from the white areas of skin.

Sources: [1]

Two different insertions at KIT

White spotting in cats is associated with an insertion of a full-length feline endogenous retrovirus in intron 1 of KIT.

Dominant White is associated with a distinct, shorter insertion at KIT, a viral LTR. White spotting and Dominant White are distinct phenotypes.

Sources: [1] [2]

Phobias · November 7, 2026

Algophobia — Intense Fear of Physical Pain

Algophobia is an extreme fear of physical pain. Fear and avoidance can reduce activity and may worsen disability and pain, though the pattern varies between people, and fear of pain does not mean the pain is imaginary.

At a glance

Meaning
Extreme fear of physical pain
Triggers
Thinking about pain, anticipated movement, reminders of painful experiences
Catastrophizing
Imagining the worst outcome
Hypervigilance
Intensely monitoring for pain or threat
Body alarm
Can include palpitations, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath
Help
CBT, and an individualized, clinician-guided gradual return to suitable activities

A clinical term for fear of pain

Algophobia is an established clinical term for an extreme fear of physical pain. The term is descriptive. It is not a claim that the fear has a separate diagnostic code.

Sources: [1]

Triggers, thoughts and body alarm

Thinking about pain, an anticipated movement, and reminders of painful experiences can trigger anxiety and avoidance. The body's alarm can include palpitations, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath.

In this context, catastrophizing means that a person imagines the worst outcome, and hypervigilance means intensely monitoring for pain or threat.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

The fear-avoidance pattern

Fear-avoidance can reduce activity and participation, and it may worsen disability and pain. The pattern varies between people.

Actual pain and fear of pain both merit assessment. A sense of threat is not a direct measure of tissue injury, and fear does not mean that pain is imaginary.

Sources: [1] [2]

Help planned with the healthcare team

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help change pain-related thoughts. An individualized, clinician-guided gradual return to suitable activities can help with fear of pain. The sources add that treatment should address the actual pain too.

Professional help is the step the sources point to when fear interferes with daily life. Treatment is planned with the healthcare team, not by forcing painful exposure.

Sources: [1] [3]

Atychiphobia — Intense Fear of Failure

Atychiphobia is an intense fear of failure. The worry can start before an event such as an exam or a job interview, and it is not the same thing as perfectionism.

At a glance

Meaning
Intense fear of failure
Example triggers
Potential failure in exams or job interviews
Possible symptoms

Fear of failure, not perfectionism

Atychiphobia means an intense fear of failure. It is an established descriptive name for a phobia, not a separate diagnostic code. Atychiphobia and perfectionism are not the same. Fear of failure differs from striving to be flawless.

Sources: [1]

What sets it off

Potential failure in an exam or a job interview can trigger the fear. Worry about failing can arise before the event itself.

Phobia symptoms can include severe worry, palpitations, trembling and feeling sick. These are possible symptoms, and they are not universal.

Sources: [1] [2]

Felt threat and avoidance

A phobia can feel genuinely threatening, and intense fear need not match the situation. A possible unsuccessful outcome is not the same as immediate physical danger.

People may avoid situations in which failure is possible. That avoidance can impair how a person performs at work or at school.

Sources: [1]

Talking therapy

Talking therapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help with phobias. The NHS guidance is to seek professional help when symptoms affect a person's life.

Sources: [2]

Autophobia — Intense Fear of Being Alone

Autophobia, also called monophobia, is an extreme fear of being alone. It is not the same as loneliness, and the fear can arise without any immediate threat.

At a glance

Meaning
Extreme fear of being alone
Also called
Monophobia
When fear occurs

Not the same as

Treatment used

An extreme fear of being alone

Autophobia is an extreme fear of being alone. Monophobia is another name for it. Cleveland Clinic describes autophobia as a specific phobic disorder, though the descriptive name is not itself a separate diagnostic code.

The fear can occur when a person is alone, when they anticipate being alone, or when they worry that people will leave.

Sources: [1]

How it differs from loneliness

Autophobia differs from loneliness. Loneliness concerns the quantity or quality of a person's connections. Autophobia involves anxiety about being alone.

A phobic fear can occur without an immediate threat, and being alone is not in itself proof of danger. That does not cancel out genuine hazards.

Sources: [1]

Body alarm and avoidance

Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, trembling, dizziness and severe worry, and they vary between people. Thinking about a feared situation can be enough to trigger anxiety or panic. Avoidance can come to organize daily life and to limit it.

Sources: [2] [3]

Treatment and clinical support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based talking treatment used for phobias. Gradual exposure is used in treatment. It is planned for the individual, with professional help where needed.

The NHS sources point to clinical support if fear interferes with daily life. Educational illustrations such as this one are not a diagnosis.

Sources: [2] [3]

Phobias · November 7, 2026

Phonophobia — Persistent Fear of Sound

Phonophobia is a persistent fear of sound. Everyday sounds such as traffic, closing doors and loud speech can set it off even at non-damaging levels, and the term is not interchangeable with hyperacusis.

At a glance

Meaning
Persistent fear of sound
Example triggers
Traffic, closing doors and loud speech, even at non-damaging levels
Autonomic arousal
Can include palpitations, sweating and trembling
Not interchangeable with
Hyperacusis
In migraine literature
Can mean sound intolerance, not a phobic disorder
Help

A word with more than one use

Phonophobia is an established clinical term for a persistent fear of sound. That is the sense used here: fear of sound, not a separately named diagnostic category.

In migraine literature the same word can mean sound intolerance and not a phobic disorder. Phonophobia and hyperacusis are also not interchangeable. Hearing-related and emotional components can overlap, and they require clinical assessment.

Sources: [1]

Sounds, anticipation and arousal

Environmental sounds such as traffic, closing doors and loud speech can trigger fear, even at non-damaging levels. Autonomic arousal can include palpitations, sweating and trembling.

Anticipation of feared sounds and learned reactions can accompany avoidance of situations that involve sound. That avoidance may restrict social participation and daily life.

Sources: [1] [2]

Fear does not measure acoustic danger

Fear is not a measurement of acoustic danger, and sounds that do no damage can trigger it. Genuinely hazardous noise is a separate matter. It should not be used for exposure.

Sources: [1]

Treatment and hearing assessment

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based talking therapy used for phobias. Professionally guided graded exposure may be part of treatment. It follows an individualized, safe plan and is not forced exposure to loud sound.

The sources point to a clinician if fear affects daily life. Painful sound or concerns about hearing merit a hearing assessment. General education is not diagnosis. The journal source is a case report, so it does not show how common phonophobia is or how treatment turns out for other people.

Sources: [1] [2]

Thermophobia — Persistent Fear of Heat

Thermophobia is a descriptive term for a persistent fear of heat. Heat can also cause actual illness, so physical symptoms must not simply be assumed to be anxiety.

At a glance

Meaning
Persistent fear of heat
Triggers
Heat-related situations and hot objects
Possible phobia symptoms
Severe worry, palpitations, trembling, dizziness and fear of losing control
Possible overheating symptoms
Heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, weakness and nausea
Treatment used
CBT, a talking therapy

How the term is used

Thermophobia is an established descriptive term for fear of heat. Heat-related situations and hot objects can trigger anxiety. A published case report uses the name for a fear involving hot food.

The word names a fear and is not a claim of a separate diagnostic category. The meaning, persistent fear of heat, was also checked in the medically edited RxList dictionary.

Sources: [1]

Symptoms and avoidance

Phobias can involve severe worry, palpitations, trembling, dizziness and a fear of losing control. Symptoms differ between people.

Avoiding feared circumstances can bring short-term relief. The cited case reports avoidance, and symptoms that subsided spontaneously. That is what happened in a single reported case. It is not a universal mechanism for all patients.

Sources: [1] [2]

Real heat risks

Heat can cause actual illness. The CDC guidance behind the infographic is to stay cool and hydrated, use shade and cooling, and take local heat-risk advice seriously.

Symptoms of overheating can include heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, weakness and nausea. Physical symptoms must not simply be assumed to be anxiety.

Sources: [2] [3]

Help for the phobia

Phobias can interfere with daily life. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a talking therapy used to treat phobias. The guidance in the sources is to seek professional help if symptoms affect a person's life.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

How they form

Internal waves are vertical disturbances within the density layers of the ocean. Tidal flow over a submarine ridge can generate them. The infographic follows that case: tidal water flows across an underwater ridge, and internal waves then propagate along the density layers.

Once generated, internal waves propagate through the ocean. They can also contribute to the mixing of water masses, which is one of the effects the infographic covers.

Reef fish · November 11, 2026

Firefish

The firefish, or red firegoby, is a small coral-reef fish that hovers just above the bottom, facing into the current to eat zooplankton. It retreats into a burrow when disturbed.

At a glance

Scientific name
Nemateleotris magnifica
Also called
Red firegoby
Reported upper size
Up to 3 inches (about 7.6 cm), approximate
Range
Tropical Indo-Pacific and Central Pacific, including East Africa to Pitcairn
Habitat
Outer reef slopes at 6 to 61 m
Diet
Zooplankton, especially copepods and other crustacean larvae

How to recognize it

The firefish, also called the red firegoby, has an elongate white first dorsal fin, a yellow snout and a white head. The body is white and grades to bright orange-red toward the rear. The fish raises and waves its long first dorsal fin, and aquarium and university sources describe this as fin signaling.

Clearwater Marine Aquarium gives a maximum size of up to 3 inches, about 7.6 cm. That is an approximate reported upper size, not a precise measurement that applies to every adult.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Where it lives

The firefish is a coral-reef fish of the tropical Indo-Pacific and Central Pacific, with a range that includes East Africa to Pitcairn. It lives on outer reef slopes at 6 to 61 m.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

Feeding in the current, hiding in burrows

The firefish often hovers within 0.5 m above the bottom, facing into the current to eat zooplankton, especially copepods and other crustacean larvae.

It uses holes in the bottom as burrows and retreats when disturbed. Adults live alone or in pairs, while several juveniles may share one hole.

Sources: [1] [3]

What this means for an aquarium

The aquarium recommendations on the infographic are inferred from the biology described by its sources. They are to supply refuges the fish can reach and suitably small planktonic foods, and to avoid large predators. Clearwater Marine Aquarium lists triggerfish, lionfish and large angelfish as threats.

Pairing in the wild is not a guarantee that any group will be compatible, and plankton feeding alone does not establish that the fish is safe in every reef tank. The infographic gives no numeric tank minimum and no blanket guarantee of safety with corals or invertebrates.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Longnose hawkfish

The longnose hawkfish is a slender reef fish with a very long, thin snout and a red cross-hatch pattern. It perches on gorgonians or black coral and feeds on zooplankton and small crustaceans.

At a glance

Scientific name
Oxycirrhites typus Bleeker 1857
Length
To 13 cm (about 5.1 inches)
Range
Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific, including the Red Sea
Perches on
Gorgonians or black coral
Reported depth

Diet
Zooplankton and small crustaceans

How to recognize it

The longnose hawkfish has a whitish body with horizontal and vertical red bands that form a cross-hatch grid. The body is slender and flattened from side to side, and the snout is very long and thin. The fish grows to 13 cm, about 5.1 inches.

Tufts of cirri sit at the tips of the dorsal spines. The lower rays of the pectoral fins are stout and elongated, and the fish uses them for perching.

Sources: [1] [2]

Where it lives and what it eats

Its marine range covers the Indo-Pacific and the eastern Pacific, including the Red Sea. It perches on gorgonians or black coral. Its reef habitat is generally deeper, with a reported total depth range of 5 to 100 m and some shallow exceptions.

The Oregon Coast Aquarium describes its food as zooplankton and small crustaceans. The pointed mouth helps it capture small prey.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

What this means for an aquarium

The aquarium points on the infographic are labeled as inferences, not tested universal compatibility. They are to provide stable structure for perching and suitable small meaty foods. Small crustacean tankmates may be prey, so the fish cannot be promised safe in every reef tank. Its association with this habitat does not prove that all corals or all companions are safe. No numeric tank minimum is given.

Reef fish · November 11, 2026

Mandarinfish

The mandarinfish is a small bottom-dwelling fish of western Pacific coral reefs and shallow lagoons. It feeds by day on tiny invertebrates, and feeding it in an aquarium can be difficult.

At a glance

Scientific name
Synchiropus splendidus
Range
Western Pacific
Habitat
Tropical coral reefs and shallow lagoons, on the bottom among coral and rubble
Reported size
6 to 9 cm in one source; a maximum of 6 cm in another
Diet
Small crustaceans and other tiny invertebrates, including copepods and worms
Skin
Scaleless, with a thick mucus coating

How to recognize it

The mandarinfish has a broad, flattened head, a small mouth and wavy blue-green and orange markings. The male has an elongated first dorsal spine, and the fanlike pelvic fins are used at the bottom. The skin has no scales and carries a thick coating of mucus. The secretion may deter predators.

Adults are small. The Aquarium of the Pacific reports 6 to 9 cm (2.4 to 3.5 inches), while the Animal Diversity Web reports a maximum of 6 cm, so there is no single agreed maximum.

Sources: [1] [2]

Where it lives and how it feeds

The mandarinfish lives on tropical coral reefs and in shallow lagoons of the western Pacific. It is a bottom dweller, found among coral and rubble.

It feeds by day on the bottom, taking small crustaceans and other tiny invertebrates, including copepods and worms. The food comes from the substrate and live rock. The fish is usually shy and mostly passive.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why aquarium care is difficult

Feeding a mandarinfish in an aquarium can be difficult, and many individuals do not accept prepared food. The implication for husbandry is to verify that a fish keeps taking suitably tiny food over time. The presence of live rock alone does not show that. Small body size does not mean easy care. Males can fight in an aquarium, so the advice is to avoid pairing males.

Reef compatibility depends on diet. Tiny invertebrates are prey, so the fish cannot be promised safe in every reef tank. That caution is an inference from the documented diet, not a blanket safety classification.

Sources: [1] [2]

Royal gramma

The royal gramma, also called the fairy basslet, is a small purple and yellow reef fish of the western Atlantic and Caribbean. It stays close to ledges, caves and overhangs and feeds mainly on planktonic crustaceans.

At a glance

Scientific name
Gramma loreto Poey, 1868
Other common name
Fairy basslet
Length
Approximately 8 cm total length (about 3 inches)
Range
Reefs of the western Atlantic and Caribbean
Habitat
Close to reef ledges, walls, caves and overhangs
Diet
Primarily planktonic crustaceans

How to recognize it

The royal gramma has an elongate body that is flattened from side to side, a large eye and a short snout. The front of the body is purple and the rear is yellow. A black spot marks the front of the dorsal fin, yellow lines radiate from the eye, and the pelvic fins have elongated rays. The fish reaches approximately 8 cm in total length, about 3 inches.

The accepted species is Gramma loreto Poey, 1868. Royal gramma and fairy basslet are both common names, and the U.S. Geological Survey reports no scientific synonyms.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Life along the ledges

This is a reef fish of the western Atlantic and Caribbean. It lives close to reef ledges, walls, caves and overhangs, and it may swim upside down with its belly facing the roof.

It feeds primarily on planktonic crustaceans. It may also remove external parasites from other fishes, but it is not an obligate cleaner. Groups on the reef are territorial and have dominance hierarchies based on size. Larger fish occupy the prime feeding positions.

Sources: [1] [3]

Nests and egg care

Males build nests in crevices and care for the eggs, which are demersal, meaning they rest on the bottom. Once the sexes have differentiated they stay separate. The species does not routinely change from female to male.

Sources: [1] [3]

What this means for an aquarium

The aquarium points on the infographic are planning implications drawn from the biology, not tested minimum standards. Shelter and feeding access should be consistent with the ledge habitat and the plankton diet. Because the fish is territorial, groups seen in the wild do not imply that a group will be compatible in an aquarium. Small fish and invertebrates can be prey, so reef-safe is not an absolute guarantee.

The species has been bred in captivity. Aquarium fish should never be released. The occurrence of this species outside its native range has been associated with possible aquarium release as well as natural expansion.

Sources: [1] [3]

Benign Prostatic Enlargement — When Bladder Outflow Narrows

Benign prostatic enlargement, or BPH, is noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that becomes more common with age. The enlarged prostate can squeeze the urethra and impede the flow of urine.

At a glance

What it is
Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate
Where the prostate lies
Below the bladder, around the urethra at the bladder neck
Cause
Uncertain; age-related hormonal changes may contribute

How outflow narrows

BPH is noncancerous enlargement of the prostate. It becomes more common with age. Its cause is uncertain, and age-related hormonal changes may contribute.

The prostate lies below the bladder and surrounds the urethra at the bladder neck. Enlargement can squeeze the urethra and impede urine flow. The bladder works harder against the narrowed outflow and may eventually fail to empty fully, leaving residual urine.

Sources: [1] [2]

Urinary symptoms

Symptoms can include difficulty starting, a weak or interrupted stream, incomplete emptying, frequency, urgency and nighttime urination. Prostate size does not reliably predict how severe the symptoms are. Other urinary disorders can cause similar symptoms and require evaluation.

Sources: [1] [2]

Evaluation and management

Evaluation includes history, examination and urine tests. Selected patients may need PSA testing, urine-flow testing or a bladder ultrasound.

Mild symptoms may be monitored. Reducing caffeine and alcohol, and shifting fluids away from bedtime while maintaining daytime hydration, may help. Alpha blockers, selected by a clinician, relax muscles in the prostate and bladder neck. Clinician-selected 5-alpha reductase inhibitors can help shrink the prostate. Procedures may relieve obstruction when symptoms are severe or medicines fail. Treatment has benefits and risks and is individualized.

Sources: [1] [2]

Urgent warning signs

Being unable to urinate, blood in the urine, or painful, urgent urination with fever and chills or severe lower abdominal pain are reasons to seek urgent medical care.

Sources: [1] [2]

Chronic Sinusitis — Inflamed Drainage Pathways

In chronic sinusitis, the lining of the sinuses is inflamed and swollen, which interferes with mucus draining into the nose and throat. It is driven more by inflammation than by infection.

At a glance

Sinuses
Air spaces behind the cheekbones and forehead, connected to the inside of the nose
Main driver

Main treatments

Antibiotics

Can make it worse

Sinuses and their drainage

Sinuses are air spaces behind the cheekbones and forehead that connect to the inside of the nose. A swollen sinus lining interferes with the drainage of mucus into the nose and throat.

Chronic sinusitis is driven more by inflammation than by infection, and antibiotics are not always helpful. Allergies, nasal polyps and asthma can accompany sinusitis and make it worse.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and evaluation

Symptoms can include facial pressure or tenderness, a blocked nose, nasal discharge and a reduced sense of smell. Prolonged or repeated symptoms warrant clinical evaluation. CT may be needed for prolonged symptoms or suspected complications, but not routinely for uncomplicated sinusitis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment

Saline nasal irrigation and nasal steroid sprays are the main treatments for the symptoms of chronic sinusitis. For irrigation at home, the NHS describes boiling the water and then cooling it before use.

Endoscopic surgery may help selected chronic cases that are not controlled by medicines. It works by widening the natural drainage pathways of the sinuses.

Sources: [1] [2]

When urgent help is needed

The reasons given for seeking urgent medical help are being very unwell, symptoms that worsen or are not helped by painkillers, and weakened immunity.

Sources: [1]

Hypertension — Pressure That Can Go Unnoticed

Hypertension is persistently high pressure of blood against the walls of the arteries. It usually has no symptoms, yet over time it can damage the heart, brain and kidneys.

At a glance

What it is
Persistently high pressure of blood against artery walls
Systolic pressure
The pressure during heart pumping
Diastolic pressure
Measured between beats, while the heart fills
Symptoms
Usually none
Organs at risk
Heart, brain and kidneys
Emergency
Above 180 systolic and/or above 120 diastolic, with symptoms

Pressure in the arteries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Hypertension means persistently high pressure of blood against the artery walls. Systolic pressure is the pressure while the heart is pumping. Diastolic pressure is measured between beats, while the heart fills.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why it goes unnoticed

High blood pressure usually has no symptoms. Measurements help establish the diagnosis. They are often repeated over visits and taken with a validated home monitor.

Over time, high blood pressure can damage the heart, brain and kidneys. It increases the risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke and kidney disease.

Sources: [1] [2]

Risk factors and care

Risk factors include family history, increasing age, excess sodium, inactivity and excess alcohol. Multiple factors can contribute. Care can include a heart-healthy DASH eating pattern, limiting sodium and alcohol, physical activity and medicines prescribed to the individual.

Sources: [1] [2]

When a high reading is an emergency

Pressure higher than 180 systolic and/or higher than 120 diastolic, together with chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, a change in vision or difficulty speaking, is an emergency. The CDC guidance is to call 911. For pressure that high without symptoms, the guidance is to contact a healthcare professional.

Sources: [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Hyperthyroidism — When Thyroid Hormone Runs Too High

Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid produces too much thyroid hormone, which speeds many body functions. Symptoms vary, and diagnosis requires clinical assessment and thyroid blood tests, not symptoms alone.

At a glance

The gland
Small, butterfly-shaped, in the front of the neck
What goes wrong
The thyroid produces too much thyroid hormone
Causes named
Graves disease (autoimmune) and overactive nodules
Blood tests
TSH, T4 and T3
Rare emergency
Thyroid storm

An overactive thyroid

The thyroid is a small butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. Its hormones regulate energy use and affect nearly every organ. Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid produces too much thyroid hormone, speeding many body functions. Graves disease is an autoimmune cause that stimulates excess hormone production. Overactive nodules are another cause.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and testing

Possible symptoms include heat intolerance, sweating, hand tremor, weight loss despite increased appetite, and a rapid or irregular heartbeat. Symptoms vary.

Diagnosis requires clinical assessment and thyroid blood tests, not symptoms alone. TSH, T4 and T3 tests help evaluate thyroid function.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Treatment options

Treatment is individualized by cause, severity and circumstances. Antithyroid drugs reduce hormone production. Beta blockers ease symptoms but do not stop hormone production. Radioiodine or surgery are options for selected patients. Radioiodine is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Sources: [1] [2]

Complications and thyroid storm

Untreated hyperthyroidism can cause heart rhythm problems and bone thinning. Thyroid storm is a rare, life-threatening emergency. A high fever, a pounding rapid heart and confusion in someone with hyperthyroidism warrant calling emergency services.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Scoliosis — A Curve With a Twist

Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine, shaped like a C or an S, in which the vertebrae also twist or rotate. Most scoliosis in adolescents is idiopathic, meaning its exact cause is unknown.

At a glance

Shape
Sideways C- or S-shaped curve, with twisted or rotated vertebrae
Regions involved
Thoracic and lumbar regions may be involved
Most adolescent cases
Idiopathic (exact cause unknown); can run in families
Not causes
Poor posture and heavy backpacks
Measuring the curve

A curve and a twist

Scoliosis can form a sideways curve shaped like a C or an S. The vertebrae also twist or rotate. The thoracic and lumbar regions of the spine may be involved. Asymmetry of the shoulders, ribs, waist and hips can be signs.

Sources: [1] [2]

What is known about the cause

Most adolescent scoliosis is idiopathic, which means its exact cause is unknown. It can run in families. Poor posture and heavy backpacks do not cause idiopathic scoliosis. Small curves are often painless and go unnoticed. Growth spurts can worsen a curve.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Examination and treatment

Clinical examination includes the forward bend test, which reveals rib asymmetry. X-rays locate and measure the curve. Treatment depends on the size and location of the curve and on how much growth remains. Many mild curves are observed. Bracing for selected growing children helps prevent a curve from progressing. It does not straighten an existing curve. Surgery may be considered for severe or progressing curves. Most children and teens can lead normal, active lives with appropriate follow-up.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Pain that needs prompt evaluation

Severe back pain, or pain with weakness or numbness in a limb, warrants prompt medical evaluation for other causes.

Sources: [3]

Tennis Elbow — The Outer Tendon Attachment

Tennis elbow, or lateral epicondylitis, is a load-related problem where a wrist extensor tendon attaches to the outer bony prominence of the elbow. Playing tennis is not required to get it.

At a glance

Also called
Lateral epicondylitis
Where it hurts
The outside of the elbow
Tendon commonly involved
ECRB wrist extensor tendon
Attachment point
Lateral epicondyle, the outer bony prominence of the humerus
Onset
Symptoms often develop gradually

The outer elbow attachment

The elbow contains the humerus, radius and ulna. The lateral epicondyle is the outer bony prominence of the humerus. Tendons connect muscle to bone. The ECRB wrist extensor tendon attaches at the lateral epicondyle and is commonly involved in tennis elbow.

Repeated vigorous use of the forearm can damage the tendon attachment, with degeneration and sometimes microscopic tears. This is not necessarily a complete tendon rupture.

Sources: [1] [2]

What brings it on

Gripping, repetitive wrist extension or twisting in work, hobbies and racquet sports can contribute. Tennis is not required, and sometimes no repetitive injury is identified.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and assessment

Symptoms include pain and tenderness on the outside of the elbow, a weak grip, and pain that is worsened by gripping or wrist movement. Symptoms often develop gradually.

Assessment uses the history of symptoms and an examination. Tests or imaging may be used to exclude other causes and are not necessarily required for everyone.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it is managed

Care includes reducing the activities that worsen symptoms. Physiotherapy with stretching and strengthening of the wrist and forearm can help, and a forearm strap or brace may ease symptoms. Surgery is considered for persistent symptoms after prolonged nonsurgical treatment. It is not an automatic first step. Pain that persists despite self-care is a reason to seek medical review.

Sources: [1] [2]

Arm pain that is urgent

A hot, swollen elbow with fever or chills, or severe pain with difficulty moving, warrants urgent assessment. An injury with deformity or snapping also needs urgent assessment. Sudden arm pain with chest pressure, heaviness or squeezing requires emergency help, and is not to be assumed to be tennis elbow.

Sources: [3]

Agouti — Pigment Bands Within a Single Hair

Agouti is the banding of pigment within a single cat hair. ASIP interacts with MC1R to switch between two pigments as the hair grows, and this banding is distinct from the tabby pattern across the coat.

At a glance

Trait
Agouti, pigment bands within a single hair
Switch
ASIP interacting with MC1R during hair growth
Pigments
Eumelanin and phaeomelanin
Banded hairs
A/A and A/a
Solid hairs
Two recessive a copies (non-agouti)

How the bands form

ASIP interacts with MC1R to switch the pigment deposited in a hair between eumelanin and phaeomelanin. The switching happens during hair growth, and it creates bands within the hair.

Sources: [1]

Bands are not stripes

Banding within a hair is distinct from the tabby pattern, which is laid out across the coat. In a brown tabby, the hairs between the dark stripes are banded. The hairs in the stripes remain dark.

Sources: [1]

How it is inherited

The genotypes A/A and A/a support agouti banding. Two copies of the recessive a produce non-agouti hairs, which are solid.

The overall appearance of a coat depends on other genes as well. Orange cats can retain tabby markings regardless of their agouti genotype.

Sources: [1] [2]

  • A/A and A/a support agouti banding; two recessive a copies produce non-agouti solid hairs. [1] [2]

Inner-Ear Balance — Rotation, Motion and Gravity

A cat's vestibular apparatus lies deep in the inner ear. Its semicircular canals respond to rotation speeding up or slowing down, and its utricle and saccule respond to straight-line motion and gravity.

At a glance

Structure
Vestibular apparatus, deep in the inner ear beside the cochlea
Semicircular canals
Three, in different planes; respond to rotational acceleration or deceleration
Utricle and saccule
Respond to linear acceleration or deceleration and gravity
Nerve
Vestibular portion of cranial nerve VIII
Reflexes
Vestibulospinal and vestibulo-ocular

Where the vestibular apparatus sits

The vestibular apparatus lies deep in the inner ear, beside the cochlea. It communicates with centers in the brainstem. The vestibular portion of cranial nerve VIII carries information from the receptors toward the brainstem.

Sources: [1] [2]

Canals that sense rotation

Three semicircular canals occupy different planes. Each has an ampulla that contains a crista with sensory hair cells. The receptors of the semicircular canals respond to rotational acceleration or deceleration, which is rotation speeding up or slowing down.

Sources: [1]

Sensing straight-line motion and gravity

The utricle and the saccule contain sensory maculae. These respond to linear acceleration or deceleration, which is motion in a straight line speeding up or slowing down, and to gravity.

Sources: [1]

What the information is used for

Vestibular information helps stabilize posture and the eyes during head movement. It does this through the vestibulospinal and vestibulo-ocular reflexes. The infographic shows the normal anatomy and how it works. It is not a chart of disease.

Sources: [1] [2]

Milk Lactose — Why the Saucer Can Upset Digestion

Many cats are lactose intolerant. They do not have enough lactase in the intestine to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, so dairy can cause digestive problems.

At a glance

Lactose

Why milk can cause trouble

Lactose is the sugar in milk. Lactase in the intestine is needed to digest it, and many cats lack enough lactase. Many cats are lactose intolerant, and dairy can cause gastrointestinal problems.

The PDSA veterinary team notes that drinking milk that contains lactose can cause vomiting, diarrhea and stomach pain. Not every cat becomes ill.

Sources: [1] [2]

Milk, water and cat milk

Adult cats do not need milk when they are fed an appropriate complete, balanced diet. Cats should always have clean, fresh water available. Reduced-lactose or lactose-free cat milk still adds calories, and it is often not a complete meal.

Sources: [1] [2]

Cat Atlas / Inside the cat · November 13, 2026

Retractile Claws — Tendon Pull and Elastic Return

A domestic cat's claw is protruded by muscle pull and retracted by elastic ligaments. The deep digital flexor muscle pulls through its tendon to protrude the claw, and the elastic ligaments retract it passively.

At a glance

Animal
Domestic cat, forepaw digits 2 to 5
Claw out
The deep digital flexor muscle contracts and pulls its tendon
Claw in
Elastic ligaments retract it passively
Ligaments
The lateral ligament is especially important; a pair of dorsal elastic ligaments
Why retract
Protects claws from wear when not in use

The bones of the digit

The distal phalanx and the middle phalanx meet at the distal interphalangeal joint. In digits 2 to 5 of the domestic cat's forepaw, the distal phalanx overlaps the middle phalanx when the claw is retracted.

Sources: [1]

Tendon pull

To protrude the claw, the deep digital flexor muscle contracts. Its tendon carries the pull to the flexor process of the distal phalanx. This protrudes the claw and stretches the elastic ligaments.

Sources: [1] [2]

Elastic return

Elastic ligaments retract the claw passively. The lateral ligament is especially important, and there is also a pair of dorsal elastic ligaments. Retraction protects the claws from wear when they are not in use.

Sources: [1] [2]

Cat Atlas / Household hazards · November 13, 2026

String Ingestion — The Linear Foreign-Body Hazard

Swallowed string can act as a linear foreign body in a cat and cause intestinal obstruction. Once the string anchors, the intestine gathers into pleats along it, and the string can erode through the intestinal wall.

At a glance

Hazard
Swallowed string acting as a linear foreign body
Where it anchors
Around the base of the tongue, or at the pylorus (stomach outlet)
What happens
The intestine gathers into pleats along the string (plication)
Possible signs
Vomiting, appetite loss and abdominal pain; presentation varies
Suspected ingestion
Needs immediate veterinary care

How a string becomes a hazard

Swallowed string can act as a linear foreign body in cats and cause intestinal obstruction. The string can anchor around the base of the tongue or at the pylorus, the outlet of the stomach.

Peristaltic movement then gathers the intestine into pleats along the anchored string. This pleating is called plication. The string can erode through the intestinal wall, which causes leakage and life-threatening peritonitis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Signs and assessment

Vomiting, loss of appetite and abdominal pain are possible signs, and the presentation varies. Suspected ingestion of a foreign object needs immediate veterinary care. Veterinarians use the history, an examination and imaging to assess it.

Sources: [1] [3]

How it is removed

Some foreign bodies in the upper digestive tract can be removed endoscopically. Linear foreign bodies often require surgery, and severely damaged bowel may require resection, the surgical removal of that part.

Sources: [1] [2]

Amaxophobia — Fear of Driving or Riding in a Vehicle

Amaxophobia is a fear of driving or riding in a vehicle. Even thinking about a journey may bring on anxiety, and feeling endangered is not proof that a crash is imminent.

Fear as driver or passenger

Amaxophobia means fear of driving or riding in a vehicle. It is a specific phobic disorder, not a separate stand-alone diagnostic category.

Sources: [1]

Anxiety ahead of a journey

Thinking about a vehicle journey may trigger anticipatory anxiety. The outcomes a person fears may include a crash or an injury. Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, sweating and trembling, which are bodily anxiety responses.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

The sense of danger

Phobias involve an exaggerated or unrealistic sense of danger. Feeling endangered is not proof that a crash is imminent.

Sources: [1] [3]

Avoidance and support

Avoiding feared situations can restrict everyday life, and continual avoidance can worsen the problem. That is a general point about phobias from the NHS trust source.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help with phobias, and gradual exposure may be used with professional support. The sources point to seeking help if symptoms affect daily life.

Sources: [2] [3]

Chionophobia — Fear of Snow

Chionophobia is an intense fear of snow. Seeing snow or wintry weather, or even thinking about a light snowfall, can trigger severe anxiety that exceeds the actual danger.

At a glance

Meaning
Intense fear of snow
Type
Natural-environment specific phobia, as Cleveland Clinic describes it
Triggers

Possible symptoms

Treatment options

A natural-environment phobia

Chionophobia means an intense fear of snow. Cleveland Clinic describes it as a specific phobia of the natural-environment type. It is not a separate named diagnostic code.

Sources: [1]

Snow, anticipation and body alarm

Seeing snow or wintry weather can trigger severe anxiety, and so can even the thought of a light snowfall. Phobias can involve anticipatory anxiety, and they can produce palpitations, trembling and dizziness.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Alarm compared with danger

Phobic alarm can exceed the actual danger. A light snowfall can provoke severe anxiety even without immediate danger. That does not imply that all winter conditions are safe. The infographic shows an imagined photographic scene, not a clinical case.

Sources: [1]

Staying indoors through winter

Phobias can bring an overwhelming urge to avoid the feared situation, which limits daily activities. Avoiding snow can mean staying indoors during winter, with disruption of work and relationships.

Sources: [1] [3]

Treatment options

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment option. Gradual exposure or desensitization is used for simple phobias. A specialist can help, and no single program works for everyone. The sources point to professional help when fear disrupts daily life.

Sources: [2] [3]

Fear of doctors and medical tests

Iatrophobia means fear of doctors. It can involve an extreme fear of doctors or of medical tests, beyond the actual danger. Cleveland Clinic describes it as a specific phobic disorder.

Sources: [1] [3]

Symptoms and possible origins

Phobia symptoms can include severe worry, palpitations, dizziness, nausea and trembling. Phobias may relate to frightening experiences, but the causes are not always clear.

Sources: [2] [3]

When fear keeps people from care

Fear may lead people to avoid necessary medical attention, even when they are sick. The infographic explains the fear through an imagined close clinical encounter, and it does not portray clinicians as dangerous.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a talking therapy used to treat phobias. The NHS guidance is to seek professional help when symptoms affect a person's life.

The same guidance says that talking to a trusted person and relaxation breathing can help manage phobia symptoms.

Pediophobia is a descriptive name for fear of dolls. Humanlike doll faces can feel uncanny or unnerving, a subjective reaction that is not evidence a doll is alive or dangerous.

The name and the uncanny face

Pediophobia is an established descriptive name meaning fear of dolls. Humanlike doll faces can be experienced as uncanny or unnerving. That is a subjective reaction. It is not evidence that a doll is alive or dangerous.

Contact, anticipation and avoidance

A phobia may cause anxiety or panic on contact with the feared object, or even when thinking about it, which is called anticipatory anxiety. Body alarm can include palpitations, trembling, dizziness and chest tightness.

Sources: [2] [3]

Treatment with specialist support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. Gradual exposure or desensitization can be part of treatment, with specialist support. The NHS sources point to professional help if fear affects daily life.

Scopophobia — Fear of Being Watched or Stared At

Scopophobia is a term for the fear of being watched or stared at, particularly by unfamiliar people. Fear of scrutiny can occur in social anxiety, and the name alone is not a diagnosis.

At a glance

Meaning
Fear of being watched or stared at, particularly by unfamiliar people
Related context
Social anxiety, in which fear of scrutiny and negative judgment can occur
Possible bodily symptoms
Sweating, trembling and rapid heart rate
Research-supported help
CBT, for social anxiety
Limit of the evidence
No treatment trial specific to scopophobia is claimed

A name, not a diagnosis

Scopophobia is a term for fear of being watched or stared at, particularly by unfamiliar people. Fear of scrutiny and of negative judgment can occur in social anxiety. The descriptive name alone is not a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Feeling scrutinized

Anxiety can arise before a social situation. Possible bodily symptoms include sweating, trembling and a rapid heart rate.

Anxiety can occur even when there is no current threat. Feeling scrutinized does not establish actual danger, and it does not establish that other people have hostile intentions. Avoidance may feel helpful in the short term, while the anxiety remains without treatment.

Sources: [2]

What the treatment evidence covers

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is supported by research for social anxiety. Exposure therapy, which progressively confronts feared situations, is part of treatment. This evidence is about social anxiety in general. No treatment trial specific to scopophobia is claimed.

The sources point to professional help when anxiety interferes with everyday life. Treatment is tailored with a qualified clinician.

How things work · November 17, 2026

Cherenkov Radiation — Outrunning Light in Water

Cherenkov radiation is light produced when an electrically charged particle travels through a transparent medium, such as water, faster than light travels in that medium. It can produce the blue or violet glow in the water around a nuclear reactor core.

At a glance

What it is
Light from a charged particle that outruns light in a transparent medium
Example particles
High-energy electrons
Seen as
A blue or violet glow in water around a nuclear reactor core
Limit not exceeded
The speed of light in vacuum
Analogies
A sonic boom or a boat bow wave
Uses
Nuclear-material accounting and particle-physics measurements

Faster than light in water

Cherenkov radiation occurs when an electrically charged particle travels faster than light travels in the transparent medium around it. Light travels more slowly in water than in vacuum. That does not allow a particle to exceed the speed of light in vacuum. High-energy electrons are one example of charged particles that can produce Cherenkov radiation.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the glow is made

The moving charged particle interacts with the medium, and the electromagnetic waves that are emitted reinforce into a shock wave of light. This emission can produce the blue or violet glow seen in the water around a nuclear reactor core.

The process can be compared with a sonic boom or with the bow wave of a boat. These are analogies, not identical phenomena. The diagrams in the infographic are conceptual and not to scale.

Sources: [1] [2]

What it is used for

Cherenkov light is used in nuclear-material accounting. It is also used in particle physics to measure the energy and trajectory of particles.

Sources: [1]

Geysers — The Boiling Feedback Engine

A geyser is a hot spring with restricted underground plumbing. Water heated under pressure begins to boil, the pressure drops, more water boils, and expanding steam drives water and vapor out of the vent.

At a glance

What it is
A hot spring whose restricted underground plumbing limits free circulation
Water source
Surface water that seeps underground
Heat source
The volcanic geothermal system
What drives the eruption
Expanding steam
Visible white plume
Largely condensed water droplets
Cone
Can be built by silica deposited from thermal water

Water heated under pressure

Geysers are hot springs whose restricted underground plumbing limits free circulation. Surface water seeps underground and is heated by the volcanic geothermal system. Pressure increases with depth, and water under pressure can remain liquid above the temperature at which it boils at the surface.

In many studied geysers, bends or side chambers in the plumbing trap steam. Bubbles released from them heat the column of water above.

Sources: [1] [2]

How an eruption starts and stops

The first boiling and overflow reduce the pressure. That allows more hot water to boil and the steam to expand. The expanding steam drives liquid water and vapor out of the vent. The visible white plume is largely condensed water droplets, not pure water vapor.

An eruption ends as the reservoir is depleted or the water cools. Replenishment and heating then permit another cycle.

Sources: [1] [2]

Varied plumbing and silica cones

The underground shapes of geysers vary. The side-chamber cutaway in the infographic is a schematic, not a surveyed map of a particular geyser. Silica deposited from thermal water can build a cone around a geyser vent.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the Hercules Beetle Uses Its Horns

Horns for squeezing and lifting

Dynastes hercules is a scarab beetle. Males bear horns on the head and on the thorax, and females lack horns. Males use the horns to squeeze and lift rivals in contests for access to females. The wing covers of males can be olive with dark spots, and females are usually black.

Life in decaying wood

The species undergoes complete metamorphosis, passing through egg, larva, pupa and adult. Larvae feed on dead wood in decaying logs. Adults generally feed on fallen, rotting fruit. The range includes southern Mexico to Bolivia and the Lesser Antilles, and it includes rainforest.

Pillow Lava — Underwater Budding Basalt

Pillow lava forms when basalt enters water. The water chills the outside of the lava into a glassy rind, and the lava grows by budding one bulbous lobe after another.

Rock
Basalt

Shape

How a pillow buds

Basalt entering water can form bulbous lobes called pillows. The water rapidly chills the outside of the lava into a glassy rind. A continued supply of lava expands the lobe until its rind cracks, and a new lobe buds out.

Sources: [1] [2]

How pillows pile up and cool

Pillows accumulate in mounds, and they settle into the gaps between earlier pillows. As the interior of a pillow cools, joints can radiate inward from its surface.

Sources: [1] [2]

A sign of former water

Ancient pillow basalts can indicate that the setting where they formed was once underwater, because these lobes take shape when basalt enters water.

Sources: [1] [2]

Southern Mole Cricket — The Underground Calling Horn

The southern mole cricket is a brown burrowing insect, native to South America and introduced to the southeastern United States. It digs with enlarged forelegs, and males call from a horn-shaped burrow opening that projects the sound skyward.

At a glance

Scientific name
Neoscapteriscus borellii, formerly Scapteriscus borellii
Body length
25 to 32 mm
Native to
South America
Introduced to
Southeastern United States
Habitat

A body built for digging

The southern mole cricket is Neoscapteriscus borellii, formerly Scapteriscus borellii. Adults are brown, with enlarged digging forelegs, forewings longer than the pronotum and hindwings that extend beyond the abdomen. Body length is 25 to 32 mm.

Neoscapteriscus has two blade-like dactyls on the tibia of each foreleg. In N. borellii they are separated at the base by at least half the basal width of a dactyl. Mole crickets force loose soil aside with strokes of the enlarged forelegs, and they spend nearly all their lives underground.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [5]

The calling burrow

Males call with a low, ringing trill from a horn-shaped burrow opening. These specialized calling burrows augment the sound and project it skyward, which attracts flying members of the same species, including females.

A generalized Neoscapteriscus calling burrow contains an opening horn, constrictions, a bulb, a turn-around, and surface and deep tunnels.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Where it lives and what it eats

The species is native to South America and has been introduced to the southeastern United States. Its habitat includes moist sandy or mucky open areas such as lawns, fields and the margins of ponds or streams. Southern mole crickets are omnivorous but largely carnivorous, and they mostly eat other insects.

Sources: [1] [2] [5]

Eggs, nymphs and generations

The eggs are gray-brown and bean-shaped, and they are laid in underground chambers. Nymphs resemble smaller, wingless adults. One generation a year is typical, except in south Florida, where there can be two. Eggs are laid in spring, and large nymphs or adults overwinter.

Sources: [1] [5]

The generalized nervous system

The infographic's nervous-system view is a generalized insect schematic, not a measured dissection of this species. In that general plan, a brain on the upper (dorsal) side connects to a nerve cord on the lower (ventral) side, which has ganglia arranged by segment. The ganglia of the thorax supply nerves to the legs and wings.

Sources: [6]

Copperband Butterflyfish — The Crevice Forager

The copperband butterflyfish, also called the beaked coralfish, is a silvery-white fish with orange-copper bars. The adult uses its long snout to extract bottom-living invertebrates from holes and crevices.

At a glance

Scientific name
Chelmon rostratus
Also called
Beaked coralfish
Maximum length

Range

Habitat

How to recognize it

The body is silvery-white with three broad orange-copper bars. A narrower orange bar with dark margins runs through the eye. The dorsal and anal fins are tall, and the dorsal fin carries an eyespot. A dark bar with blue edging crosses the base of the tail. The maximum length is 20 cm, or 8 inches.

Chelmon rostratus is the accepted species name. Copperband butterflyfish and beaked coralfish are both common names for this fish.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Where it lives

The copperband butterflyfish has a tropical Indo-West Pacific range. It lives along rocky shores, on coral reefs, in estuaries and on silty inner reefs, at a preferred depth of 1 to 25 m. It is encountered singly or in pairs, and it forms pairs during breeding.

Sources: [1] [2]

A snout for holes and crevices

The adult's long snout extracts bottom-living invertebrates from holes and crevices. The long snout develops after the larva has settled.

Sources: [1] [2]

In an aquarium

The Georgia Aquarium describes this fish as difficult to keep in home aquariums. It is sometimes used to control Aiptasia.

Its diet of bottom-living invertebrates and its occasional use against Aiptasia do not establish that it is safe for every reef tank. Compatibility and feeding need to be assessed, and pest control cannot be promised. This is a cautious husbandry implication of the documented diet, not a claim that all individuals eat the same ornamental animals.

Sources: [2]
