Flame Angelfish — Fire in the Reef’s Shelter

The flame angelfish is an orange-red fish with black vertical bars from western and central Pacific reefs. It is secretive, stays close to shelter and feeds mainly on bottom algae and detritus.

At a glance

Scientific name
Centropyge loriculus
Range
Scattered reef localities in the western and central Pacific
Habitat
Rich lagoon and seaward coral reefs at 5 to 60 m
Wild diet
Mainly bottom algae and detritus
Typical captive size
About 4 inches (approximately 10 cm), according to a producer
Sex change
Females can change into males

How to recognize it

Typical flame angelfish have orange-red bodies with an orange-yellow midbody, black vertical bars and a dark blotch behind the pectoral fin. Blue and purple streaks highlight the rear of the dorsal and anal fins. The tail fin has light orange-yellow rays with translucent membranes, and the pelvic fins are orange-red.

Sources: [1] [5]

Where it lives

The species occurs across scattered reef localities in the western and central Pacific, including Palau, the Marshall Islands and the Society Islands. Its habitat is rich lagoon and seaward coral reefs at 5 to 60 m. It is a secretive fish that stays close to shelter. Its primary foods in the wild are algae growing on the bottom and detritus.

Sources: [1]

Harems and sex change

Flame angelfish are protogynous, which means females can change into males. Wild males maintain harems, and spawning typically occurs at dusk.

Sources: [1]

Guidance from an aquaculture producer

The husbandry guidance comes from Biota, an aquaculture producer. Biota describes a typical captive size of about 4 inches (approximately 10 cm), which is not a species maximum. It recommends an aquarium of at least 65 US gallons (approximately 246 liters) for adults. That is a producer guideline, not a universal threshold.

Biota recommends varied, nutritious food and frequent feeding. The fish also pick at rockwork for algae and sponges. They are territorial with their own species and with other dwarf angels.

Biota rates the fish reef safe with caution. Individuals may pick at soft corals, clams and fleshy large-polyp stony corals, and feeding does not establish guaranteed coral safety.

Sources: [5]

Planning a tank, and never releasing

Shelter-rich rockwork and algae-based food reflect the shelter association and grazing biology of the species in the wild. Aquarium space and compatibility need individual planning. Aquarium fish should never be released. The U.S. Geological Survey identifies probable aquarium release among the pathways by which this species has been introduced.

Sources: [1] [5]

Orchid Dottyback — The Red Sea’s Violet Crevice Hunter

The orchid dottyback is a small purple fish known only from the Red Sea. It darts from reef ledges to feed on passing zooplankton and returns to shelter, and the male tends the eggs in a nook or cave.

At a glance

Scientific name
Pseudochromis fridmani Klausewitz, 1968
Family
Pseudochromidae
Range
Known only from the Red Sea
Recorded maximum length
6.3 cm total length, about 2.5 inches
Habitat
Vertical rock faces or beneath overhangs, with small holes for refuge
Diet
Passing zooplankton

How to recognize it

The orchid dottyback is a purple to magenta fish. A black line through the eye is its diagnostic mark. Under aquarium lighting the fish shows purple. In the wild, the filtering of red light can make fish in deeper water appear blue. The recorded maximum total length is 6.3 cm, about 2.5 inches.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Life on Red Sea rock faces

The species is known only from the Red Sea. It is a marine, reef-associated fish that lives on vertical rock faces or beneath overhangs and takes refuge in small holes. It darts out from reef ledges to feed on passing zooplankton, then returns to shelter.

Sources: [1] [2]

Eggs in nooks and caves

The eggs form a mass held by filamentous threads. The mass is deposited in nooks or caves and tended by the male.

Captive breeding is established. One published study of captive fish found an incubation of approximately 96 hours at 27 ± 1 degrees Celsius. That is the result of one study, not a universal timer.

Sources: [2] [5]

In an aquarium

The aquarium guidance comes from the culture and care notes of ORA, Biota and Proaquatix. Foods for cultured fish include mysid and brine shrimp, krill, pellets and flakes. The fish is moderately territorial and should have many hiding places. It may fight others of its own species and similar-looking fish. Being more peaceful than many other dottybacks does not mean it is free of aggression.

It is generally compatible with corals but may chase very small shrimp, so reef-safe is not a guarantee for every small mobile invertebrate. Biota suggests a tank size of 30 US gallons, approximately 114 liters. That is husbandry guidance, not a biological threshold from the wild.

Sources: [2] [3] [4]

Pajama Cardinalfish — The Twilight Coral Refuge

The pajama cardinalfish is a small western Pacific fish that hides among branching corals by day and leaves them at night to feed on small crustaceans. The male incubates the eggs in his mouth.

At a glance

Scientific name
Sphaeramia nematoptera (Bleeker, 1856)
Family
Apogonidae
Also called
Coral cardinalfish
Maximum reported length
8.5 cm, about 3.3 inches
Habitat
Western Pacific lagoons, bays and sheltered coastal coral reefs
Diet
Small shrimps, crabs and other small crustaceans

How to recognize it

The pajama cardinalfish, also called the coral cardinalfish, has a yellow head, large red eyes and two dorsal fins. A vertical black bar runs beneath the first dorsal fin, and large brown spots mark the rear of the body. The maximum reported length is 8.5 cm, about 3.3 inches.

Sources: [1] [2]

Life among branching corals

This fish lives in the western Pacific, in lagoons, bays and sheltered coastal coral reefs. The Oregon Coast Aquarium records depths to 14 m. It lives among branching corals, including Porites cylindrica, Acropora and Anacropora.

It forms social groups. The fish hide by day and leave the protection of the coral to feed at night. The species is a carnivore that feeds on small shrimps, crabs and other small crustaceans.

Sources: [1] [2]

Eggs carried in the mouth

The male incubates the fertilized eggs in his mouth and does not feed during incubation. No precise length of incubation is given.

Sources: [1] [2]

In an aquarium

The aquarium guidance comes mainly from a care guide by Coralife, a manufacturer. The fish is described as generally peaceful toward other tankmates and as reef safe. That does not imply safety for every small crustacean, since crustaceans are its natural prey. Groups can develop dominance hierarchies and need a larger aquarium with ample cover.

The guide advises a varied meaty diet. Some fish refuse dry foods at first. They can be coaxed with frozen food and later weaned to dry, and feeding at night is worth trying for reluctant feeders. Coralife lists a minimum of 20 US gallons (approximately 76 liters). That is not presented as a universal recommendation for housing groups, which need more room and cover.

Sources: [1] [3]

Yellow Tang — The Reef’s Golden Grazer

The yellow tang is a lemon-yellow reef fish of the subtropical Pacific. It grazes algae from rocks by day, rests in crevices at night and carries a defensive spine on each side of its tail base.

At a glance

Scientific name
Zebrasoma flavescens
Adult size
About 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches)
Native range
Subtropical Pacific, including Hawaii and western Pacific islands toward Japan
Reef depth
Includes 2 to 46 m
Diet
Algae grazed from rocks and reef framework
Defense
A white spine on each side of the tail base

How to recognize it

The yellow tang has an oval, lemon-yellow body that is flattened from side to side, with large dorsal and anal fins and a small, downturned mouth. A white defensive spine sits on each side of the base of the tail. Adults grow to about 15 to 20 cm, or 6 to 8 inches.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Where it lives

Its native range is the subtropical Pacific, including Hawaii and western Pacific islands toward Japan. It lives on reefs, at depths that include 2 to 46 m. Individuals may occur alone or in loose groups, and juveniles can be territorial.

Sources: [1] [3]

Grazing by day, resting at night

The yellow tang grazes algae from rocks and the reef framework with flexible, comb-like teeth and its small downturned mouth. This grazing helps limit the competition between algae and coral.

Grazing is a daytime activity. At night the fish rests alone in reef crevices, and its color is grayish-yellow with a white band along the side.

Sources: [1] [2]

The blades at the tail base

The blades at the base of the tail are modified scales that sit in slots. Flexing the tail exposes them. The fish uses them in defense and in competition. They can inflict deep wounds, so touching the fish is to be avoided.

Sources: [2]

What this means for an aquarium

The aquarium notes on the infographic are qualitative inferences from the biology, not numeric husbandry prescriptions. They point to algae-based feeding and reef-like refuges for the night. Because of territorial behavior, grouping in the wild is not a guarantee of peaceful tankmates. Grazing around coral is not, on its own, a guarantee that the fish is compatible with every reef tank.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

The yellow watchman goby is a small yellow goby of sandy bottoms that shares a burrow with an alpheid shrimp. The shrimp builds and maintains the burrow, and the goby guards it and warns of approaching predators.

The yellow watchman goby, also called the yellow shrimp goby and the banded prawn goby, is yellow with fine pale blue or white spots on the head and upper body. Faint brown bars can occur. The yellow phase and the whitish barred phase are the same species. The fish can reach about 10 cm, approximately 4 inches.

Sources: [1] [4]

Where it lives

This is a marine goby of the eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific. It lives on the sandy bottoms of seagrass beds, lagoons and sheltered coral reefs, at 2 to 15 m depth in the Oregon Coast Aquarium account.

A burrow shared with a shrimp

The goby shares its burrow with an alpheid shrimp. The shrimp builds and maintains the burrow. The goby guards it and warns of approaching predators, and the two communicate by touch and movement.

The aquarium guidance comes from a care guide by Coralife, a manufacturer. It recommends varied meat-based foods and says this bottom-feeding fish can learn to feed in mid-water. The Oregon Coast Aquarium account lists algae and bivalves, so no universal claim about its diet is made.

Inguinal Hernia — Abdominal Wall Passage

An inguinal hernia is a bulge of abdominal contents, often fat or small intestine, through a weak area of the lower abdominal wall at the groin. Most patients need surgical repair, and strangulation requires emergency care.

At a glance

What it is
Abdominal contents bulging through a weak area of the lower abdominal wall
Where

Contents

Types

Emergency

A passage through the abdominal wall

An inguinal hernia is abdominal contents bulging through a weak area of the lower abdominal wall at the groin. The contents often include fat or small intestine. The peritoneum forms a sac around the hernia. The inguinal canals are passages through the lower abdominal wall.

Indirect hernias relate to an opening present at birth. Direct hernias relate to weakness of the wall that develops later. Family history and aging are associated with increased risk. Chronic cough, constipation and repeated heavy lifting may contribute through increased abdominal pressure.

Sources: [1]

Symptoms and diagnosis

A groin bulge, aching, burning or heaviness may worsen with coughing, straining, lifting or prolonged standing and improve when lying down. Clinical history and examination are used for diagnosis. Imaging may help when the diagnosis is unclear.

Sources: [1] [2]

Repair or watchful waiting

Most patients need surgical repair. Open or laparoscopic repair may use mesh to reinforce the weak area. Watchful waiting, with regular medical follow-up, may be appropriate for some men with few or no symptoms. That is not advice for everyone.

Sources: [1]

Trapped and strangulated hernias

Incarceration means the contents are trapped. Strangulation means the blood supply is cut off, and it requires emergency care. Sudden severe pain, a bulge that is suddenly larger or newly irreducible, fever, redness, nausea or vomiting are reasons to seek urgent medical help. Obstruction may cause bloating.

Sources: [1]

Ménière Disease — Inner Ear Episodes

Ménière disease is an inner-ear condition whose symptoms come and go: spinning vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus and ear fullness. Its underlying cause remains unclear, and there is no cure yet.

At a glance

Part affected
Inner ear, usually one ear
Symptoms
Spinning vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, sometimes nausea or vomiting
Pattern
Symptoms come and go
Associated finding
Endolymph buildup (endolymphatic hydrops)
Cause
Underlying cause remains unclear
Cure
None yet

Inside the inner ear

The labyrinth of the inner ear contains the cochlea, for hearing, and the semicircular canals and otolith organs, including the utricle and saccule, for balance. The membranous labyrinth contains endolymph.

A buildup of endolymph, called endolymphatic hydrops, is associated with disrupted hearing and balance signals in Ménière disease. Its underlying cause remains unclear.

Sources: [1]

Episodes of symptoms

Symptoms come and go. They are spinning vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, and sometimes nausea or vomiting. Usually one ear is affected.

Sources: [1] [2]

Diagnosis and management

Diagnosis uses the history of symptoms and hearing testing, with evaluation for other causes. There is no single definitive test.

There is no cure yet. Medicines directed by a clinician may help the symptoms of an attack, hearing aids may help hearing loss, and vestibular rehabilitation may help persistent balance problems. Reducing salt in the diet is something to discuss with a clinician. It may help some people, but it is not a cure.

Sources: [1] [2]

Driving and stroke warning signs

The NHS guidance is not to drive during dizziness or when vertigo is coming on. Vertigo with new facial droop, arm weakness or speech difficulty may be a stroke, and the guidance is to call emergency services immediately.

Sources: [2]

Peripheral Arterial Disease — Leg Blood Flow

Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) commonly involves plaque building up in arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the legs and feet. It can cause leg pain with walking, and some people have no symptoms.

At a glance

What narrows
Arteries, commonly from plaque buildup
Where flow drops
Legs and feet
Typical symptom
Leg muscle pain with walking that eases after a few minutes of rest
Muscles commonly affected
Calves
Test
Ankle-brachial index, comparing blood pressure at the ankle and arm
Associated risk
Higher heart attack and stroke risk

Narrowed arteries in the leg

Arteries carry blood away from the heart. PAD commonly involves a buildup of plaque that narrows arteries and reduces blood flow to the legs and feet. The infographic shows a schematic of the arterial supply of the leg, with a magnified view of an artery narrowed by plaque and reduced flow beyond it. It does not present a vein or a clot as the usual cause. PAD is associated with a higher risk of heart attack and stroke.

Sources: [1] [2]

Pain with walking

Intermittent claudication is leg muscle pain with walking that eases after a few minutes of rest. The calves are commonly affected. Some people have no symptoms. Other symptoms can include cold feet, weakness or numbness, and sores that do not heal.

Sources: [1] [2]

Evaluation and management

Evaluation includes clinical assessment and an ankle-brachial index, which compares blood pressure at the ankle and the arm.

Management may include an exercise program guided by a clinician, stopping smoking, prescribed medicines and, in selected cases, procedures to improve blood flow. The guidance also covers controlling blood pressure and cholesterol and, for people with diabetes, managing blood sugar and looking after the feet.

Sources: [2]

Acute limb ischemia

Acute limb ischemia is an emergency. A foot that is paler or colder than the other, being unable to feel or move the foot, or pain or pins and needles at rest requires immediate medical help. The guidance is to call 911.

Sources: [3]

Arginine — The Ammonia Detoxification Link

Arginine is an essential amino acid that cats must get from their diet. It takes part in detoxifying ammonia, which is released when protein is broken down.

At a glance

Nutrient
Arginine, an essential amino acid
Role
Takes part in ammonia detoxification
Pathway

Why diet matters
Cats make only limited arginine in their own bodies
Deficiency
Can cause ammonia accumulation, vomiting, neurological signs and potentially death

What arginine is

Arginine is an essential amino acid and a building block of proteins. Cats require it in their diet. They can make only limited amounts of arginine in their own bodies, so they depend on the supply from food.

Sources: [1] [2]

The ammonia link

The breakdown of protein releases ammonia, and arginine takes part in detoxifying it. The urea cycle converts ammonia to urea, with arginine as an important intermediate. The infographic explains this with a simplified metabolic schematic.

Sources: [1] [2]

Deficiency and diet

Arginine deficiency can cause ammonia to accumulate, with vomiting, neurological signs and potentially death. A carefully formulated, complete feline diet accounts for these special nutrient requirements. An all-meat diet is not balanced.

Sources: [1] [2]

Siamese Points — Temperature and Growing Fur

The darker face, ears, legs and tail of a Siamese cat follow skin temperature. Pigment is produced more readily in cooler skin and inefficiently at the warmer skin temperatures of the trunk.

At a glance

Pattern
Darker face, ears, legs and tail in a seal-point Siamese

Warmer trunk skin

Pigment that depends on temperature

Siamese pigmentation is associated with variants of the tyrosinase gene, TYR. In Siamese cats, pigment production is inefficient at the warmer skin temperatures of the trunk. It occurs more readily in cooler skin.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why the points are dark

In a seal-point Siamese, the face, ears, legs and tail are normally cooler than the central body, and they are darker. These darker areas are the points of the coat pattern.

Sources: [1]

Fur that grows back darker

When body fur is lost in cold conditions, the exposed skin is cooler. As the fur grows back, that cooler skin can produce darker replacement fur.

Sources: [1]

The Cautious Investigator — Exploring from Cover

Cats need protection from things they perceive as dangers, including unfamiliar environments. A secure retreat helps a cat feel protected, and how a cat responds to an unfamiliar object varies from one cat to another.

Need

Why a retreat matters

Cats need protection from perceived dangers, and unfamiliar environments are among them. A secure retreat helps a cat feel protected.

A safe place may be a cardboard box or a carrier. It has sides that surround the cat, and the cat is able to enter and leave. Raised safe places are often preferred.

Sources: [1]

Smells, sounds and sudden objects

Cats use smell to evaluate their surroundings. Unfamiliar smells or sounds can be stressful. The sudden appearance of a novel object may provoke a startle response. Individual cats differ, and fearful cats may react more strongly.

The Cornell source says not to startle cats deliberately with surprise objects. A frightened cat can associate the event with the place where it happened or with the person involved.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the picture does and does not show

The infographic illustrates a cat that may observe, approach and retreat. These are possible responses. They are not a sequence that every cat must follow, and they are not a diagnosis. Individual responses vary.

Sources: [1] [2]

The Third Eyelid — A Protective Fold

The third eyelid, or nictitating membrane, is a whitish-pink membrane at the inner corner of a cat's eye. It extends across the eye to help protect it from scratches, and its glands contribute to the watery part of tears.

At a glance

Location

Where it sits

The nictitating membrane is the cat's third eyelid. It is a whitish-pink membrane that lies beneath the other eyelids, at the inner corner of the eye near the nose.

The cornea is the clear dome at the front of the eye. The iris is the colored area that surrounds the pupil.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it protects the eye

The third eyelid extends across the eye to help protect the eyeball from scratches. The infographic shows this extension as a schematic. It does not show a timed, voluntary wink.

Sources: [1]

Tears and blinking

Glands within the third eyelid contribute to the watery portion of tears. The upper and lower eyelids blink and spread tears over the surface of the eye. This keeps the surface moist and clears small particles.

Sources: [1] [2]

When a veterinarian is needed

The infographic shows the normal third eyelid. The Cornell source says to seek veterinary care for a cat with apparent eye discomfort and discharge.

Cat Atlas / Household hazards · November 20, 2026

The Tilt-Window Trap — Compression in a Narrowing Gap

A bottom-hung window that tilts inward creates a narrowing gap at its side. A cat can become trapped there, and the compression of blood vessels and nerves is potentially life-threatening.

At a glance

Window type
Bottom-hung, tilting inward
The trap
A narrowing gap at the side
Where cats are caught
Between the last rib and pelvis, or by a hindlimb
What is compressed
Blood vessels and nerves
Possible result
Hindlimb weakness or paralysis
Urgency
Potentially life-threatening; requires urgent veterinary attention

How a cat gets trapped

Bottom-hung windows tilt inward and create a narrowing gap at the side, in which cats can become trapped. A cat's attempts to escape can cause it to slide downward in the gap. The cat may be caught between the last rib and the pelvis, or the entrapment may involve a hindlimb.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the compression does

Compression of blood vessels reduces blood flow to the muscles, nerves and spinal cord. Direct compression of nerves also contributes to the injury. Neurological injury may cause weakness or paralysis of the hindlimbs.

Sources: [1] [2]

When blood flow returns

The restoration of blood flow can cause reperfusion injury, with further tissue damage and serious complications that affect the whole body. Window entrapment is potentially life-threatening and requires urgent veterinary attention.

Sources: [1] [2]

  • Compression of blood vessels reduces blood flow to muscles, nerves and spinal cord; direct nerve compression also contributes to injury. [1] [2]
  • Neurological injury may cause hindlimb weakness or paralysis. [1] [2]
  • Restoration of blood flow can cause reperfusion injury with further tissue damage and serious systemic complications. [1]

Phobias · November 21, 2026

Anthophobia — Flowers Too Close

Anthophobia is an extreme fear of flowers. Any flower, specific types, or parts such as petals, leaves or stems may trigger it, even though the fear concerns something unlikely to cause harm.

At a glance

Meaning
Extreme fear of flowers
Described as
A specific phobic disorder
Possible triggers
Any flower or specific types; petals, leaves or stems; thinking about flowers
Possible bodily symptoms
Palpitations, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath
Treatment
Gradual exposure therapy guided by a mental health professional, often combined with CBT

What can trigger it

Anthophobia means an extreme fear of flowers. Any flower may trigger the fear, or only specific types. Parts, including petals, leaves or stems, may trigger it too.

It is described as a specific phobic disorder. The word is a descriptive name for a fear, and it is not a claim of a separate diagnostic category.

Sources: [1]

Body alarm and actual danger

Thinking about flowers can trigger anxiety. Possible bodily symptoms include palpitations, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath. Phobic fear concerns something unlikely to cause harm, and an intense feeling of alarm is not itself proof of actual danger.

Sources: [1] [2]

Avoidance and professional treatment

Avoiding flowers can restrict work and social life and make leaving home difficult. The sources point to professional help when phobia symptoms affect daily life.

A mental health professional can guide gradual exposure therapy. It is often combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to change perceptions and responses.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Entomophobia — When an Insect Feels Too Close

Entomophobia is a fear of insects. Seeing insects or thinking about them can provoke extreme fear or anxiety that is out of proportion to the likely real-life harm.

At a glance

Meaning
Fear of insects
Type
Specific phobia
Triggers
Encounters indoors or outdoors, images, and fears of bites or stings
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, trembling, chest tightness and dizziness
Recommended treatment
CBT

Fear out of proportion to harm

Entomophobia means fear of insects. Seeing insects, or thinking about them, can provoke extreme fear or anxiety. It is a specific phobia.

The fear is out of proportion to the likely real-life harm. It is not proof that an encounter with an insect is dangerous.

Sources: [1]

Triggers, symptoms and avoidance

Triggers can be encounters indoors or outdoors, images, and fears of bites or stings. Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, trembling, chest tightness and dizziness. Avoidance may restrict outdoor exercise, events or leaving home.

Sources: [1] [2]

What CBT involves

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a recommended treatment for phobias. A therapist helps a person examine thoughts, feelings and actions, and change avoidance, in an individualized plan. The NHS guidance is to seek professional help when symptoms affect daily life.

Sources: [2] [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Treatment

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. Professional help is appropriate when symptoms affect a person's life.

Microphobia means an extreme fear of small things. It is described as a specific phobia, not a separately named diagnostic category.

Thoughts of little things can provoke severe anxiety. The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, and most small everyday things cause no harm. The infographic depicts this felt threat with an imagined small-object trigger.

California Coastal Upwelling

Along the California coast, winds blowing along the shore can drive surface water offshore. Cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below to replace it, a process called coastal upwelling.

At a glance

Driver
Alongshore winds
What rises
Deeper, cold, nutrient-rich water
Supports
Marine productivity and fisheries
Weather link
Cold coastal water contributes to San Francisco summer fog

How the water rises

Coastal upwelling is driven by wind. Winds blowing along the shore can drive surface water offshore. Deeper water then rises to replace the surface water that has been displaced. The rising water is cold and rich in nutrients. In this way upwelling brings cold, nutrient-rich water to the California coast.

Sources: [1]

Productivity and fisheries

California coastal upwelling supports marine productivity, and it supports fisheries as well. The infographic presents these as ecological consequences of the wind-driven process.

Sources: [1] [2]

Cold water and summer fog

Upwelling brings cold water to the California coast. That cold coastal water contributes to the summer fog of San Francisco.

Sources: [1] [2]

Elephant Mosquito, Tree-Hole Predator

The elephant mosquito, Toxorhynchites rutilus septentrionalis, is a predatory mosquito. Its larvae hunt other mosquito larvae in water-filled tree holes and containers, and the adults feed on nectar, not blood.

A predator in tree holes

Toxorhynchites rutilus septentrionalis is a predatory mosquito found north to Connecticut and southern New York. Its larvae inhabit water-filled tree holes and containers, where they prey on mosquito larvae. They locate prey by its movement. The larva's mouth brushes grasp the prey, and its mandibles are powerful.

Sources: [1] [2]

The nectar-feeding adult

Adults feed on nectar, not blood, using a strongly curved proboscis. They bear iridescent scales and can exceed 7 mm in body length.

Sources: [1] [2]

Life stages and body plan

Egg, larva, pupa and adult are the stages of complete metamorphosis in flies. Insects have a head, thorax and abdomen and three pairs of legs. The generalized insect anatomy in the infographic includes a digestive tube, a heart, spiracles and branching breathing tubes.

Sources: [3]

Horseshoe Crab Blue Blood

Horseshoe crab blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-containing hemocyanin. Its clotting responds to bacterial endotoxins, and LAL is used to test medical products for them.

Body

Why the blood is blue

Horseshoe crabs are marine arthropods. They have an exoskeleton and jointed appendages. Their blood is blue. The color comes from hemocyanin, which contains copper and carries oxygen in the blood.

Sources: [1] [2]

Blood that responds to bacteria

The clotting of horseshoe crab blood responds to bacterial endotoxins. LAL is used to test medical products for endotoxins.

NOAA Ocean Today and the Smithsonian National Zoo both report that scientists are exploring synthetic alternatives to LAL. The infographic covers both the copper-based transport of oxygen and the detection of endotoxin in horseshoe crab blood.

Nature & science · November 24, 2026

Lichens — Two Kingdoms, One Body

A lichen is a stable partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner: green algae, cyanobacteria or both. The fungus gives the lichen most of its characteristics, and the partner supplies sugars made by photosynthesis.

At a glance

Partners
A fungus and a photobiont (green algae and/or cyanobacteria)
Green-algal photobiont
About 90% of lichens
Dominant partner
The fungus
Growth forms
Crustose, foliose and fruticose
Water and nutrients
Absorbed from air and rain
Use in science
Monitoring air quality

A fungus and its partner

A lichen is a stable symbiotic partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, called the photobiont. The photobiont is green algae, cyanobacteria or both. About 90% of lichens use a green-algal photobiont, and some lichens have both green algae and cyanobacteria. The photobiont photosynthesizes and supplies sugars, a source of carbon, to the fungus. The partnership is thought to be a mutualism.

The fungus is the dominant partner. It gives the lichen most of its characteristics, including the shape of its body (the thallus) and its fruiting bodies. By protecting its photobiont, the fungus lets lichens live in dry, sunny places where algae alone could not, recharging with occasional rain.

Sources: [1] [3]

Inside the thallus

Lichens have no roots, stems, leaves, waxy cuticle or vascular tissue. They absorb water and nutrients from air and rain. They are not mosses: mosses are plants with leaf-like structures, and lichens are not plants.

The thallus is layered. On the outside is a cortex of tightly packed fungal cells. Beneath it is an algal layer, and then a medulla of loosely packed, threadlike fungal filaments. When a lichen is wet, the cortex cells become transparent and the color of the algal layer shows through. Green algae often make a wet lichen bright green.

Rhizines are fungal filaments from the medulla that attach the lichen to its surface. They do not move water or nutrients as roots do. Some foliose lichens attach by one central holdfast. These are the umbilicate lichens, such as rock tripe.

Sources: [1] [2]

Three main growth forms

Lichens have three main growth forms. Crustose lichens are pressed against the surface like a crust. Foliose lichens are leafy, with distinct upper and lower sides. Fruticose lichens are hair-like, shrubby or cup-like.

Sources: [2] [3]

How lichens reproduce

The fungus produces spores from fruiting bodies. A new fungus must then find a compatible photobiont partner. Lichens also reproduce vegetatively. Soredia are granules of algae and fungi intertwined for dispersal. Isidia are vegetative outgrowths. Fragments of a lichen can also grow into new thalli.

Sources: [2]

Lichens and air quality

Lichens absorb pollutants such as heavy metals and sulfur from the air, so scientists use them to monitor air quality. Old man's beard (Usnea longissima) is an indicator of air pollution.

Sources: [1] [2]

  • Rhizines are fungal filaments from the medulla that attach the lichen to its surface; they do not move water or nutrients like roots. [2]
  • Some foliose lichens attach by one central holdfast (umbilicate lichens, such as rock tripe). [2]
  • Three main growth forms: crustose (pressed against the surface like a crust), foliose (leafy, with distinct upper and lower sides), fruticose (hair-like, shrubby or cup-like). [2] [3]
  • The fungus produces spores from fruiting bodies; a new fungus must find a compatible photobiont partner. [2]
  • Lichens also reproduce vegetatively: soredia are granules of algae and fungi intertwined for dispersal, isidia are vegetative outgrowths, and fragments can grow into new thalli. [2]
  • By protecting its photobiont, the fungus lets lichens live in dry, sunny places where algae alone could not, recharging with occasional rain. [1]
  • Lichens absorb pollutants such as heavy metals and sulfur from the air, so scientists use them to monitor air quality; old man's beard (Usnea longissima) is an air-pollution indicator. [1] [2]
  • Lichens are not mosses: mosses are plants with leaf-like structures, while lichens are not plants. [1]

Oak Leafrolling Weevil, the Leaf-Bedroll Builder

The oak leafrolling weevil is a small, shiny black weevil with one red spot on each wing cover. The adult cuts an oak leaf, lays an egg on it and rolls it into a neat cylinder, called a nidus, where the larva feeds.

At a glance

Scientific name
Synolabus bipustulatus (synonym Attelabus bipustulatus)
Adult length
Less than 1/4 inch
Color
Shiny black, with one red spot on each wing cover
Leaf roll
Called a nidus, Latin for nest
Recorded host trees
Leafrolling weevils: 16 species of oak and 2 species of chestnut
Recorded in
Eastern US oak woodlands, including Massachusetts, Connecticut and North Carolina

How to recognize it

The oak leafrolling weevil, Synolabus bipustulatus (synonym Attelabus bipustulatus), is a small, stout, shiny black weevil with one red spot on each wing cover. Adults are less than 1/4 inch long. A similar oak leaf-rolling weevil, Homoeolabus analis, is orange-red with a black head and legs.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Rolling the leaf

The adult chews slits on either side of the leaf's midrib and lays an egg near the tip of the leaf. The leaf is folded along the midrib and rolled into a neat cylinder, with the egg near the center of the roll. The egg is tiny and shaped like a rugby ball. The finished leaf roll is called a nidus, which is Latin for nest.

The larva is a legless, curved, plump grub with a brown head. It feeds on the leaf tissue inside the roll, out of reach of predators. It pupates inside the roll, and a new adult emerges. There may be more than one generation a year.

The thief weevil, Pterocolus ovatus, preys on eggs and is a kleptoparasite of the nidus. Its attelabid hosts include this species, listed under the synonym A. bipustulatus.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Host trees and range

Leafrolling weevils have been recorded on 16 species of oak and 2 species of chestnut. They are rarely pests and typically do not cause noticeable damage to their host trees.

The oak leafrolling weevil is recorded in oak woodlands of the eastern US, including Massachusetts, Connecticut and North Carolina. Its distribution is slightly more northerly than that of Homoeolabus analis, and it is not found in Florida.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

The generalized insect body plan

The internal view in the infographic is a simplified schematic of a generalized insect, not a dissection of this species. The gut has a foregut, midgut and hindgut, and most digestion and absorption occur in the midgut. Malpighian tubules, which handle excretion, join the gut where the midgut meets the hindgut.

The dorsal vessel, or heart, pumps blood through an open body cavity. Air enters through spiracles and travels through branching tracheae. The nervous system has a brain in the head, which processes sensory information, and a ventral nerve cord of ganglia. The fat body stores energy.

Wheel Bug, the Cog-Crested Predator

The wheel bug is a gray to brown assassin bug with a toothed, cog-like crest on the adult's thorax. It seizes insects with its front legs, injects digestive enzymes through a piercing beak and sucks up the liquefied tissue.

At a glance

Kind of insect
Assassin bug
Adult length

The crest and the body

The wheel bug, Arilus cristatus, is an assassin bug. The adult has a toothed crest on its thorax that resembles a cog, and a gray to brown body. Adults measure about 1 to 1.25 inches.

Wheel bugs occur across North America, including the United States, Mexico and Guatemala. They live among vegetation, including trees and shrubs.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it feeds

Wheel bugs prey on insects, including caterpillars. The enlarged front legs seize the prey. The piercing beak injects digestive enzymes, and the bug then sucks up the liquefied tissue.

Sources: [1]

Eggs and nymphs

Egg clusters are laid on twigs in fall. They overwinter and hatch in spring. The nymphs are red and black, and they lack the crest of the adult.

Sources: [1]

The generalized internal view

The internal anatomy in the infographic is simplified and generalized for insects. Spiracles lead to branching tracheae. The gut includes a foregut, midgut and hindgut. A dorsal vessel moves hemolymph, and a ventral nerve cord links the ganglia.

Coral Beauty

The coral beauty, Centropyge bispinosa, is a small angelfish of outer reef slopes. It grazes algae by day, shelters in reef crevices at night and is only conditionally suited to a reef aquarium.

At a glance

Scientific name
Centropyge bispinosa
Size
Adults can reach 10 cm, about 4 inches
Range
Tropical Indo-West and Central Pacific
Habitat
Outer reef slopes with crevices, at 5 to 45 m
Diet
Mainly grazed algae, with plankton and some worms or small crustaceans
Reef aquarium

How to recognize it

The coral beauty is a small angelfish with a laterally compressed body. Its head and its dorsal, anal and caudal fins are blue-purple, and the middle of the body is orange-yellow with blue lines or spots. Adults can reach 10 cm, about 4 inches.

FishBase lists Centropyge bispinosa as the accepted name, with the synonyms Holacanthus bispinosus and Centropyge bispinosus and the misspelling Centropyge hispinosus.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Where it lives

The species occurs in the tropical Indo-West and Central Pacific, from East Africa to Japan, Australia and the Tuamotu Islands. It lives on outer reef slopes, uses reef crevices for shelter and is found singly or in small groups. The Australian Museum reports depths of 5 to 45 m.

Sources: [1]

Food and daily routine

Grazing on algae is central to its diet. The fish is omnivorous and also takes plankton and some worms or small crustaceans. It feeds during the day and shelters in reef crevices at night. Its feeding territories can lead to mild aggression.

Sources: [1] [2]

In an aquarium

The aquarium guidance comes from an industry care sheet for dwarf angelfish in general, published by the Ornamental Aquatic Trade Association. It recommends a mature, filtered aquarium with plentiful rockwork for cover. Most dwarf angelfish do not tolerate their own or similar species, so the advice is to keep one unless the system is particularly large, has visual barriers and expert compatibility advice has been taken.

Compatibility with a reef aquarium is conditional. Some individuals nip corals and clams, so the fish cannot be guaranteed reef safe. For food, the care sheet suggests varied vegetable matter such as nori together with appropriate meaty frozen feeds, and many dwarf angelfish accept pellets and flakes. Ammonia and nitrite should be zero, and salinity and water quality should be monitored.

Sources: [4]

Flame Hawkfish

The flame hawkfish is a small scarlet fish of shallow tropical Pacific reefs. It lives among the branches of live Pocillopora and Stylophora corals, and adults eat small crustaceans.

At a glance

Scientific name
Neocirrhites armatus
Family
Cirrhitidae
Maximum reported length
9 cm total length, approximately 3.5 inches
Range
Pacific, from the Ryukyu Islands to the Line Islands and Mangareva
Typical depth

Adult diet
Small crustaceans

How to recognize it

The description rests on an adult photographed by Tanya Dewey. That fish has a scarlet body, a dark marking on the upper back and dorsal area, a black ring around the eye, a short snout and a deep, compact body.

The maximum reported total length is 9 cm, approximately 3.5 inches. That is not a guaranteed size for every adult.

Sources: [1] [3]

Where it lives

The flame hawkfish has a Pacific range from the Ryukyu Islands to the Line Islands and Mangareva, and south to the Great Barrier Reef and the Austral Islands. It is a reef-associated fish of shallow tropical habitat, with a typical depth range of 1 to 10 m.

It lives among the branches of live Pocillopora and Stylophora corals. When approached, it retreats deep into the coral.

Sources: [1] [2]

What it eats

Adults eat small crustaceans. A dietary DNA study from Moorea identified a broad assemblage of prey. That result does not make the fish an obligate eater of coral polyps, and it does not show that all prey living with coral are eaten equally.

Sources: [1] [2]

What this means for an aquarium

The flame hawkfish is a commercially kept species that requires well-oxygenated water. Refuge and oxygenation are recommendations informed by its habitat. Because this fish eats small crustaceans, small ornamental crustaceans should not be assumed safe with it. That precaution is inferred from diet. It is not a quantified aquarium trial or a universal reef-safe label.

Taking refuge in coral in the wild does not by itself prove that the fish is compatible with every reef tank. Livestock and individual behavior need to be assessed, and harmlessness to every tank mate cannot be asserted.

Sources: [1] [2]

Forceps Butterflyfish

The forceps butterflyfish probes reef crevices with an elongated jaw, plucking small prey and tearing pieces from larger invertebrates. Its feeding biology matters when considering aquarium compatibility.

At a glance

Scientific name
Forcipiger flavissimus
Family
Chaetodontidae
Reported maximum
22 cm total length
Habitat
Exposed seaward reefs and lagoon reefs
Social pattern
Usually pairs, also alone or in small groups

Recognizing the forceps butterflyfish

Forcipiger flavissimus, also called the yellow longnose butterflyfish, has a tall, flattened yellow body and a very long, pointed snout. The upper head is black and the lower head is silvery-white. A black spot marks the anal fin near the tail base, and the gill cover has a curved margin.

Forcipiger longirostris is a distinct species with an even longer snout and an angular gill cover. The reported maximum total length of the forceps butterflyfish is 22 cm, not a typical adult size.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Life around reef crevices

Its range stretches from the Western Indian Ocean to the Eastern Pacific, including Hawaii. It is common on exposed seaward reefs and also occurs on lagoon reefs. Fish are usually seen in pairs, although individuals and small groups also occur.

The elongated jaw probes coral branches and reef crevices. The mouth can open widely enough to tear pieces from larger prey, including worm tentacles and sea-urchin tube feet. It also plucks small crustaceans and fish eggs, and eats hydroids.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Aquarium compatibility needs caution

Invertebrate feeding means ornamental invertebrates may be at risk in an aquarium. Living on wild reefs does not guarantee compatibility with a reef aquarium. This is a caution based on feeding biology, not a claim that every individual eats coral or that any individual is universally reef safe.

OATA industry guidance for butterflyfish calls for mature filtration, slow additions of fish, and ammonia and nitrite levels of zero. It recommends testing water quality, monitoring salinity, and checking suitable aquarium size with a knowledgeable retailer. No species-specific tank capacity is prescribed here.

Sources: [1] [2] [5]

Green Chromis

The green chromis is a small, pale blue-green reef fish that feeds on plankton above branching coral and retreats into the branches for shelter.

At a glance

Scientific name
Chromis viridis (Cuvier, 1830)
Family
Pomacentridae
Largest reported length
10 cm (about 4 inches)
Range
Tropical Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea
Habitat
Sheltered reef flats and lagoons, 1 to 20 m deep
Diet
Plankton, taken by day

How to recognize it

The green chromis has a pale blue-green, iridescent body that is flattened from side to side, with visible scales, translucent fins and a deeply forked tail. Its small mouth sits at the tip of the snout and can extend forward. A similar fish, C. atripectoralis, has a distinct black patch at the base of its pectoral fin. The green chromis does not.

The largest reported total length is 10 cm, about 4 inches. Other guides give smaller maximums, so that figure is an upper limit, not a typical adult size.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Where it lives

This is a fish of the tropical Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea. It keeps to sheltered reef flats and lagoons, at reported depths of 1 to 20 m. Large groups gather above branching Acropora coral and retreat into the branches for shelter. Juveniles stay closely tied to coral heads.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Feeding and nesting

The green chromis feeds by day on plankton. It takes both phytoplankton and zooplankton, including copepods, by pushing its mouth forward.

The male prepares a nest and guards the eggs, which are attached to the bottom. He fans them with his tail fin to keep water moving over them.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

In an aquarium

The aquarium notes on the infographic come from a trade care sheet for chromis and damselfish, not from studies of wild fish. It advises open swimming space with rockwork for cover. Chromis are generally peaceful with peaceful species but may squabble, so check compatibility instead of expecting a harmonious school.

Feed a quality flake or pellet with suitable frozen foods, and avoid overfeeding. Ammonia and nitrite should be zero, in a mature, filtered system. Corals may change the water conditions a tank needs, and schooling in the wild does not make a fish safe for every reef tank.

Sources: [5]

Midas Blenny

The Midas blenny is a golden-orange Indo-Pacific reef fish. It swims up from the bottom to feed on zooplankton in open water and shelters in crevices in rock or coral.

At a glance

Scientific name
Ecsenius midas
Also called
Midas Combtooth Blenny
Maximum reported length
13 cm total length (about 5.1 inches)
Range
Indo-Pacific, from the Gulf of Aqaba and southeast Africa to the Marquesas
Habitat

Diet

How to recognize it

The Midas blenny has an elongated body with golden-orange coloration. Adults have a long tail, and a narrow dark margin runs along the front of the dorsal fin. The maximum reported total length is 13 cm, about 5.1 inches.

A hatchery that documents the species describes a golden-yellow body, a blunt face, large blue eyes, comb-like teeth and an eel-like way of swimming.

Sources: [1] [4]

Where it lives

Its Indo-Pacific range runs from the Gulf of Aqaba and southeast Africa to the Marquesas. It lives on coral reefs with moderate currents, from coastal reefs to outer walls, at a reported depth of 2 to 40 m. It shelters in crevices in rock or coral.

Sources: [1] [4]

Feeding in open water

The Midas blenny feeds on zooplankton while swimming 2 to 3 m above the bottom. It can change color when it moves from the bottom into open water, and it may swim with similarly colored anthias.

Sources: [1]

Husbandry notes from a hatchery

The husbandry notes come from the hatchery Sustainable Aquatics. It reports feeding a prepared hatchery diet, Spirulina brine and mysis. It advises rockwork and a tight-fitting lid, because the fish can jump.

The hatchery describes the fish as reef-safe and generally peaceful, but potentially territorial toward its own kind or fish with similar body shapes. Compatibility is to be assessed individually, not guaranteed. The hatchery recommends at least 30 US gallons, approximately 114 liters, with larger preferable to reduce aggression. That is a husbandry recommendation, not a universal biological threshold.

Acute Otitis Media

Acute otitis media is an infection of the middle ear with swelling and fluid behind the eardrum. Children are especially vulnerable because their eustachian tubes drain less easily.

At a glance

Site
Middle ear, behind the eardrum
Causes
Bacteria or viruses, often after an upper respiratory infection
Assessment
Symptoms and an examination of the eardrum

Why fluid becomes trapped

The ear canal ends at the eardrum. Beyond it, the middle ear contains the malleus, incus and stapes, which transmit sound vibrations toward the inner ear. The eustachian tube connects this space to the upper throat and helps supply air, drain fluid and maintain pressure.

In children, this tube is smaller and more level. Swelling or mucus during a cold can impede drainage. Acute otitis media involves infection and swelling, unlike an outer ear canal infection. Fluid without infection is called otitis media with effusion. It may remain after an infection, and persistent fluid can affect hearing.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and clinical assessment

Ear pain, fever, fussiness, ear tugging and difficulty sleeping can occur. Symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis. Clinicians ask about symptoms and examine the eardrum with an otoscope. A red, bulging eardrum can indicate infection; pneumatic otoscopy can check its movement for fluid.

Many middle ear infections improve without antibiotics. Clinician-directed watchful waiting or delayed prescribing may suit mild cases, while severe or persistent cases may need antibiotics. Pain or fever relief is selected with a healthcare provider for the child’s age and size.

Sources: [1] [2]

When care is needed

Medical care is needed for worsening symptoms, ear discharge, hearing loss, fever of 102.2°F (39°C) or higher, or symptoms lasting more than 2 to 3 days. A baby under 3 months with fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs medical attention right away.

Recommended flu and pneumococcal vaccines, clean hands and avoiding secondhand smoke help reduce risk. These measures do not guarantee prevention.

Sources: [2]

Bronchiectasis

Bronchiectasis leaves damaged airways widened and less able to clear mucus. Repeated infections can cause further damage, while treatment aims to manage symptoms and prevent worsening.

At a glance

Affected structures
Airways in the lungs
Main symptoms
Persistent cough, mucus and frequent chest infections
Confirmation
A specialist may use a CT scan
Treatment goal
Manage symptoms and prevent worsening

When mucus stays behind

Bronchiectasis damages the airways that carry air through the lungs, leaving them widened, loose and scarred. Damaged airways clear mucus poorly; retained mucus allows harmful bacteria to grow, and repeated infections can cause further airway damage. Possible causes include severe lung infection and immune system problems; for many people the cause is unclear.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and assessment

Main symptoms include a persistent cough, coughing up mucus and frequent chest infections; breathlessness and tiredness can also occur. Symptoms overlap with other conditions. Assessment can include mucus testing, lung function testing and blood tests; a specialist may use a CT scan to confirm the diagnosis.

Sources: [2]

Managing the condition

Bronchiectasis cannot usually be cured. Treatment aims to manage symptoms and prevent worsening, with a care plan tailored by the clinical team. A specialist physiotherapist teaches airway-clearance breathing techniques; devices may help clear mucus. Antibiotics treat chest infections when indicated by the care team. Exercise and recommended vaccinations can help manage the condition and reduce infection risk; avoiding smoking is recommended.

Sources: [2]

When urgent care is needed

Small blood streaks in mucus, worsening breathlessness or chest infection symptoms warrant urgent medical assessment. Severe breathing difficulty or coughing up more than a few spots or streaks of blood requires emergency care.

Sources: [2]

Bursitis

Bursitis is inflammation of the small fluid-filled sacs that cushion moving tissues around joints. It can cause aching pain, tenderness, warmth and swelling.

At a glance

Structure
Fluid-filled cushioning sac
Common sites
Shoulders, elbows, hips and knees
Typical symptoms
Aching pain, warmth, tenderness and swelling

A cushion under pressure

Bursae cushion between bone and moving muscles, tendons or skin. Bursitis is inflammation of these small fluid-filled sacs. It commonly affects the shoulders, elbows, hips and knees. A blow or fall, repeated motion, or prolonged pressure from leaning on elbows or kneeling can cause it.

Pain is often a dull ache and may worsen with movement or pressure. The area can become tender, warm and swollen. Redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

Sources: [1] [2]

Assessment and treatment

A clinician examines the affected area. Fluid sampling may test for infection or gout; blood tests or scans may also be used. Management may include rest from aggravating activities and pressure, wrapped ice packs and pain relief. Many cases settle within a few weeks.

Infection-related bursitis may need antibiotics. Steroid injections may reduce swelling but are not given if infection is the cause. Aspiration may ease symptoms.

Sources: [2]

When symptoms need assessment

Fever or chills, inability to move the joint, very severe pain, or symptoms persisting or worsening after 1 to 2 weeks of self-care warrant medical assessment. Padding during kneeling and regular breaks from pressure-producing activities may help prevent recurrence.

Sources: [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Tinnitus — Sound Without an External Source

Tinnitus is sound perceived without an external source. Its causes are not fully understood, but assessment can identify treatable problems and therapies can reduce its impact.

At a glance

Perception
Ringing, buzzing, hissing or humming
Pattern
Intermittent or constant
Common association
Hearing loss
Assessment
Ear examination and hearing assessment

Sound without an outside source

Most tinnitus is subjective, meaning only the affected person hears it. The sound may occur in one or both ears or in the head, and may come and go or remain constant. Tinnitus may affect sleep, concentration and mood, but it is usually not a sign of a serious medical problem.

Sources: [1] [2]

Links and an uncertain mechanism

Hearing loss and loud noise exposure are linked to tinnitus. Earwax, ear infection and some medications can also be associated. The exact causes are not fully understood. One leading theory is that inner-ear damage changes nerve signals to sound-processing brain regions, including the auditory cortex. This is not a universal proven mechanism. The cochlea is the inner-ear structure that senses sound.

Sources: [1] [2]

Assessment and symptom management

Evaluation includes an ear examination, medical and medication history, and hearing assessment. Specialist evaluation or imaging may be appropriate, especially for pulsating tinnitus. Treating an identifiable underlying cause may reduce symptoms.

Hearing aids can help when hearing loss is present. Sound therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy can reduce the impact of tinnitus, without promising a cure. There is currently no cure for tinnitus and no medication specifically for treating it.

Sources: [1] [2]

When assessment is urgent

Tinnitus that beats with the pulse needs urgent assessment. Tinnitus after a head injury, or with sudden hearing loss, facial weakness or vertigo, warrants emergency evaluation.

Sources: [2]

Trigger Finger

Trigger finger causes painful catching or locking when a flexor tendon cannot glide smoothly through the pulley at the base of a finger or thumb.

At a glance

Also called
Stenosing tenosynovitis
Main mechanism
A size mismatch between the flexor tendon and A1 pulley
Symptoms
Catching, locking, pain and stiffness
Assessment
Usually symptom history and hand examination

Where the tendon catches

Flexor tendons connect muscles in the forearm to finger bones. On the palm side, they pull the fingers into a fist. Pulleys hold these tendons close to the bones. The A1 pulley sits in the palm at the base of the finger.

A tendon may thicken or develop a bump, and the A1 pulley may thicken and narrow. This size mismatch prevents smooth gliding. Movement can then cause painful catching or locking.

Sources: [1]

Symptoms and assessment

Trigger finger may cause clicking, popping, a tender lump at the finger base, or a finger stuck in a bent position. Stiffness and locking can be worse in the morning or after inactivity. Diagnosis usually relies on symptom history and a hand examination rather than X-rays.

Many cases have no clear cause. Diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis are associated with greater likelihood, as is repetitive gripping or pinching. These associations do not establish a cause in every case.

Sources: [1] [2]

Management depends on symptoms

Some cases improve on their own. Options include reducing aggravating activities, a straight-finger splint, pain relief and a clinician-administered steroid injection. Surgical release opens the A1 pulley to give the tendon more room. Surgery may be considered for severe symptoms, failed treatment or a finger that cannot be straightened.

Persistent symptoms or difficulty with daily activities warrant clinical assessment. A finger that cannot be straightened needs medical evaluation rather than forced manipulation. This information is general education, not individualized treatment.

Sources: [1] [2]
